This edition of George Etherege’s Restoration comedy She Would if She Could takes the 1668 quarto of the play as the basis of its critical text. All spelling has been mordernized using US English spelling conventions. All interventions made by the editor that do not appear in the original edition have been marked in between brackets; any changes made to the original text have been listed in the edition’s critical apparatus at the end of the play.
For reference and citation purposes, this edition numbers speeches within each scene; for instance, the suggested reference form for the first speech in the play is 1.1.sp1.

div.head: Notes on the Text and the Play
div.p: The play was first performed by the Duke’s Company at the Lincoln’s Inn Fields’ theatre on February 6th 1668, the year it was also first released in print. Notably, King Charles II was in attendance for the premiere, as was Samuel Pepys, who described Etherege’s comedy as “silly” and said that there was “nothing in the world good in it and few people pleased in it”. Etherege himself was not all to happy with the show either, but he lay the blame — according to Pepys — on the actors, who were “out of humour and had not their parts perfect”.

Despite Pepys’ (and apparently everybody else’s) low opinion of the play, She Would if She Could was quite popular both among readers and London’s theatregoing public of the Restoration and the Enlightenment. First published in 1668, it was subsequently re-issued in 1671, 1693, 1710 and 1711. Moreover, since its premiere in 1668 the play remained a staple of the London theatre scene until the middle of the eighteenth century, the last recorded performance taking place on January 7th 1751. After more than two centuries away from the English commercial stages, Etherege’s comedy was revived at the York Arts Centre in March 1976.

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: Enter Courtall and Freeman, and a servant brushing Courtall.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: So, so, 'tis well. Let the coach be made ready.

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: It shall, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well, Frank, what is to be done today?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Faith, I think we must e'en follow the old trade: eat well and prepare ourselves with a bottle or two of good Burgundy, that our old acquaintance may look lovely in our eyes; for, for ought as I see, there is no hopes of new.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well! This is grown a wicked town; it was otherwise in my memory. A gentleman should not have gone out of his chamber but some civil officer or other of the game would have been with him and have given him notice where he might have had a course or two in the afternoon.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Truly, a good motherly woman of my acquaintance t'other day, talking of the sins of the times, told me with tears in her eyes that there are a company of higgling rascals who — partly for themselves but more especially for some secret friends — daily forestall the markets. Nay, and that many gentlemen who formerly had been persons of great worth and honor are of late, for some private reasons, become their own purveyors, to the utter decay and disencouragement of trade and industry.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I know there are some weary merchants who never trust their business to a factor. But, for my part, I hate the fatigue, and had rather be bound to back my own colts and man my own hawks than endure the impertinencies of bringing a young wench to the lure.

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Sir, there is a gentlewoman below desires to speak with you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Ha! Freeman, this may be some lucky adventure!

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: She asked me if you were alone.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: And did not you say aye?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: I told her I would go see.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
Go, go down quickly, and tell her I am! [Exit Servant.]
Frank, prithee let me put thee into this closet a while.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Why, may not I see her?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: On my life thou shalt have fair play, and go halves if it be a purchase that may with honor be divided. You may overhear all, but for decency’s sake, in, in man.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Well, good fortune attend thee.

div2.stage: [Exit Freeman into the closet.] Enter Mrs Sentry.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Mrs Sentry! This is a happiness beyond my expectation.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Your humble servant, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I hope your lady's come to town?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Sir Oliver, my lady, and the whole family. Well! We have had a sad time in the country; my lady's so glad she's come to enjoy the freedom of this place again, and I dare say longs to have the happiness of your company.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Did she send you hither?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Oh no, if she should but know that I did such a confident trick she would think me a good one, i’faith. The zeal I have to serve you made me venture to call in my way to the Exchange to tell you the good news, and to let you know our lodgings are in James Street at the Black Posts, where we lay the last summer.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Indeed, it is very obligingly done.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: But I must needs desire you to tell my lady that you came to the knowledge of this by some lucky chance or other, for I would not be discovered for a world.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Let me alone, I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Sir Oliver Cockwood, sir, is come to wait on you.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: O heaven! My master! My lady and myself are both undone, undone!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Sdeath, why did you not tell him I was busy?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: For heaven’s sake, Mr Courtall, what shall I do?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
Leave, leave trembling and creep into the wood-hole here. (She goes into the wood-hole.) (Enter Sir Oliver.)
Sir Oliver Cockwood!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Honest Ned Courtall! By my troth I think thou tak'st me for a pretty wench, thou hugst me so very close and heartily.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Only my joy to see you, Sir Oliver, and to welcome you to town.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Methinks, indeed, I have been an age absent, but I intend to redeem the time. And how stand affairs, prithee now? Is the wine good? Are the women kind? Well, faith, a man had better be a vagabond in this town than a justice of peace in the country; I was e'en grown a sot for want of gentleman-like recreations! If a man do but rap out an oath, the people start as if a gun went off. And if one chance but to couple himself with his neighbor’s daughter — without the help of the parson of the parish — and leave a little testimony of his kindness behind him, there is presently such an uproar that a poor man is fain to fly his country. As for drunkenness, 'tis true it may be used without scandal, but the drink is so abominable that a man would forbear it for fear of being made out of love with the vice.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I see, Sir Oliver, you continue still your old humor and are resolved to break your sweet lady's heart.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: You do not think me sure so barbarously unkind to let her know all this! No, no, these are secrets fit only to be trusted to such honest fellows as thou art.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well may I, poor sinner, be excused since a woman of such rare beauty, such incomparable parts, and of such an unblemished reputation is not able to reclaim you from these wild courses, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: To say the truth, she is a wife that no man need be ashamed of, Ned.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I vow, Sir Oliver, I must needs blame you, considering how tenderly she loves you.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Aye, aye, the more is her misfortune. And mine too, Ned: I would willingly give thee a pair of the best coach horses in my stable so thou couldst but persuade her to love me less.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Her virtue and my friendship sufficiently secure you against that, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I know thou wert never married, but has it never been thy misfortune to have a mistress love thee thus entirely?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: It never has been my good fortune, Sir Oliver. But why do you ask this question?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Because then, perchance, thou mightst have been a little sensible what a damned trouble it is.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: As how, Sir Oliver?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Why look thee, thus. For a man cannot be altogether ungrateful: sometimes one is obliged to kiss, and fawn, and toy, and lie fooling an hour or two, when a man had rather, if it were not for the disgrace sake, stand all that while in the pillory pelted with rotten eggs and oranges.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This is a very hard case indeed, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: And then the inconvenience of keeping regular hours. But above all, that damned fiend Jealousy does so possess these passionate lovers that I protest, Ned, under the rose be it spoken, if I chance to be a little prodigal in my expense on a private friend or so, I am called to so strict an account at night that for quietness’ sake I am often forced to take a dose of cantharides to make up the sum.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Indeed, Sir Oliver, everything considered you are not so much to be envied as one may rashly imagine.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, a pox of this tying man and woman together, for better, for worse! Upon my conscience it was but a trick that the clergy might have a feeling in the cause.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I do not conceive it to be much for their profit, Sir Oliver, for I dare lay a good wager: let 'em but allow Christian liberty, and they shall get ten times more by christenings than they are likely to lose by marriages.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Faith, thou hast hit it right, Ned. And now thou talkst of Christian liberty, prithee let us dine together today and be swingingly merry, but with all secrecy.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I shall be glad of your good company, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I am to call on a very honest fellow, whom I left here hard by making a visit, Sir Joslin Jolly, a kinsman of my wife’s and my neighbor in the country. We call brothers, he came up to town with me and lodgeth in the same house. He has brought up a couple of the prettiest kinswomen, heiresses of a very good fortune: would thou hadst the instructing of 'em a little. Faith, if I am not very much mistaken they are very prone to the study of the mathematics.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I shall be beholding to you for so good an acquaintance.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: This Sir Joslin is in great favor with my lady, one that she has an admirable good opinion of, and will trust me with him anywhere. But to say truth, he is as arrant a sinner as the best of us, and will boggle at nothing that becomes a man of honor. We will go and get leave of my lady, for it is not fit I should break out so soon without her approbation, Ned.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: By no means, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Where shall we meet about an hour hence?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: At the French House or the Bear.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: At the French House, by all means.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Agreed, agreed.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Would thou couldst bring a fourth man.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What think you of Frank Freeman?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: There cannot be a better — well — servant, Ned, servant, Ned!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your servant, Sir Oliver. Mrs Sentry!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: (In the hole) Is he gone?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Aye, aye! You may venture to bolt now.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: (Crawling out) O heavens! I would not endure such another fright.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, prithee be composed.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I shall not be myself again this fortnight; I never was in such a taking all the days of my life. To have been found false, and to one who to say truth has been always very kind and civil to me. But above all, I was concerned for my lady's honor—

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, there's no harm done.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Ah! Mr Courtall, you do not know Sir Oliver so well as I do. He has strange humors sometimes, and has it enough in's nature to play the tyrant but that my lady and myself awe him by our policy.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well, well, all's well. Did you not hear what a taring blade Sir Oliver is?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Ah! 'tis a vile dissembling man. How fairly he carries it to my lady's face! But I dare not discover him for fear of betraying myself.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well, Mrs Sentry, I must dine with 'em, and after I have entered them with a beer glass or two, if I can I will slip away, and pay my respects to your lady.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: You need not question your welcome, I assure you, sir. your servant, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your servant, Mrs Sentry. I am very sensible of this favor, I assure you.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I am proud it was in my power to oblige you, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
Freeman! Come, come out of thy hole. [Enter Freeman from the closet.]
How hast thou been able to contain?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Faith, much ado, the scene was very pleasant. But above all, I admire thy impudence, I could never have had the face to have wheedled the poor knight so.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Pish, pish, 'twas both necessary and honest. We ought to do all we can to confirm a husband in the good opinion of his wife.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Pray how long, if without offence a man may ask you, have you been in good grace with this person of honor? I never knew you had that commendable quality of secrecy before!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You are mistaken, Freeman, things go not as you wickedly imagine.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Why, hast thou lost all sense of modesty? Dost thou think to pass these gross wheedles on me too? Come, come, this good news should make thee a little merrier. Faith, though she be an old acquaintance she has the advantage of four or five months absence. 'Slid, I know not how proud you are, but I have thought myself very spruce ere now in an old suit that has been brushed and laid up a while.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Freeman, I know in cases of this nature thou art an infidel. But yet methinks the knowledge thou hast of my sincere dealing with my friends should make thee a little more confiding.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: What devilish oath could she invent to fright thee from a discovery?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Wilt thou believe me if I swear, the preservation of her honor has been my fault, and not hers?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: This is something.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why then, know that I have still been as careful to prevent all opportunities, as she has been to contrive 'em. And still have carried it so like a gentleman, that she has not had the least suspicion: she is the very spirit of impertinence, so foolishly fond and troublesome that no man above sixteen is able to endure her.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Why did you engage thus far then?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Some conveniences which I had by my acquaintance with the sot her husband made me extraordinary civil to her, which presently by her ladyship was interpreted after the manner of the most obliging women. This wench came hither by her commission today.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: With what confidence she denied it!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Nay, that's never wanting, I assure you. Now is it expected I should lay by all other occasions and watch every opportunity to wait upon her. She would by her good will give her lover no more rest than a young squire that has newly set up a coach does his only pair of horses.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Faith, if it be as thou say'st I cannot much blame the hardness of thy heart. But did not the oaf talk of two young ladies?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well remembered, Frank. And now I think on't, 'twill be very necessary to carry on my business with the old one, that we may the better have an opportunity of being acquainted with them. Come, let us go and bespeak dinner, and by the way consider of these weighty affairs.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Well, since there is but little ready money stirring, rather than want entertainment I shall be contented to play a while upon tick.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: And I, provided they promise fair, and we find there's hopes of payment hereafter.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Come along, come along.

div2.head: SCENE 2

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: 'Tis too late to repent. I sent her, but yet I cannot but be troubled to think she stay's so long. Sure if she has so little gratitude to let him, he has more honor then to attempt anything to the prejudice of my affection— Oh, Sentry, are you come?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Oh madam! There has been such an accident!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Prithee do not fright me, wench—

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: As I was discoursing with Mr Courtall, in came Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh! I'm ruined! Undone forever!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: You'll still be sending me on these desperate errands.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I am betrayed, betrayed by this false— what shall I call thee?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Nay, but madam, have a little patience—

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I have lost all patience, and will never more have any—

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Do but hear me, all is well—

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Nothing can be well, unfortunate woman.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Mr Courtall thrust me into the wood-hole.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: And did not Sir Oliver see thee?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: He had not the least glimpse of me.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Dear Sentry! And what good news?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: He intends to wait upon you in the afternoon, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I hope you did not let him know I sent you.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: No, no, madam, I’ll warrant you I did everything much to the advantage of your honor.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Ah Sentry! If we could but think of some lucky plot now to get Sir Oliver out of the way.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: You need not trouble yourself about that, madam, he has engaged to dine with Mr Courtall at the French House, and is bringing Sir Joslin Jolly to get your good will. When Mr Courtall has fixed 'em with a beer glass or two, he intends to steal away and pay his devotion to your ladyship.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Truly he is a person of much worth and honor!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Had you but been there, madam, to have overheard Sir Oliver's discourse, he would have made you bless yourself. There is not such another wild man in the town. All his talk was of wenching, and swearing, and drinking, and tearing.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
Aye, aye, Sentry, I know he'll talk of strange matters behind my back. But if he be not an abominable hypocrite at home, and I am not a woman easily to be deceived, he is not able to play the spark abroad thus, I assure you. (Enter Sir Oliver and Sir Joslin, Sir Joslin singing.)
My dearest dear, this is kindly done of thee to come home again thus quickly.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Nay, my dear, thou shalt never have any just cause to accuse me of unkindness.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Sir Joslin, now you are a good man, and I shall trust you with Sir Oliver again.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Nay, if I ever break my word with a lady I will be delivered bound to Mrs Sentry here, and she shall have leave to carve me for a capon.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Do you think I have a heart cruel enough for such a bloody execution?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Kindly spoke, i'faith, girl, I'll give thee a buss for that.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Fye, fye, Sir Joslin! This is not seemly in my presence.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: We have all our failings, Lady, and this is mine: a right bred greyhound can as well forbear running after a hare when he sees her as I can mumbling a pretty wench when she comes in my way.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I have heard indeed you are a parlous man, Sir Joslin.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: I seldom brag, lady, but for a true cock of the game little Joslin dares match with the best of 'em.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Sir Joslin's merry, my dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Aye, aye, if he should be wicked, I know thou art too much a gentleman to offer an injury to thine own dear lady.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Faith, madam, you must give my brother Cockwood leave to dine abroad today.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I protest, Sir Joslin, you begin to make me hate you too. Well, you are e'en grown as bad as the worst of 'em, you are still robbing me of the sweet society of Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, come, your discipline is too severe, i'faith, lady.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Sir Oliver may do what he pleases, sir, he knows I have ever been his obedient lady.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Prithee, my dear, be not angry: Sir Joseph was so earnest in his invitation, that none but a clown could have refused him.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Aye, Aye, we dine at my uncle Sir Joseph Jolly's, lady.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Will you be sure now to be a good dear and not drink nor stay out late?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p:
I'll engage for all, and if there be no harm in a merry catch or a waggish story— (Enter Ariana and Mrs Gatty.)
Ha, ha! Sly-girl and Mad-cap, are you got up? I know what you have been meditating on. But never trouble your heads, let me alone to bring you consolation.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We have often been beholding to you, sir. For every time he's drunk, he brings us home a couple of fresh servants.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, farewell my dear. Prithee do not sigh thus, but make thee ready, visit and be merry.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I shall receive most satisfaction in my chamber.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, come along, brother. Farewell one and all, lady and Sly-girl, Sly-girl and Mad-cap, your servant, your servant—

div2.stage: Exit Sir Oliver and Sir Joslin singing.

p.seg: Sentry, is the new point I bought come home, and is everything in a readiness?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Everything, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Come, come up quickly then, girl, and dress me.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Dost not thou wonder, Gatty, she should be so strangely fond of this coxcomb?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Well, if she does not dissemble, may I still be discovered when I do. Didst thou not see how her countenance changed as soon as ever their backs were turned, and how earnestly she whispered with her woman? There is some weighty affair in hand, I warrant thee. My dear Ariana, how glad am I we are in this town again!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: But we have left the benefit of the fresh air, and the delight of wandering in the pleasant groves.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Very pretty things for a young gentlewoman to bemoan the loss of indeed, that's newly come to a relish of the good things of this world.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Very good, sister!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Why, hast not thou promised me a thousand times to leave off this demureness?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: But you are so quick.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Why, would it not make any one mad to hear thee bewail the loss of the country? Speak but one grave word more and it shall be my daily prayers thou mayest have a jealous husband and then you'll have enough of it, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: It may be, if your tongue be not altogether so nimble, I may be conformable. But I hope you do not intend we shall play such mad reaks as we did last summer?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: 'Slife, dost thou think we come here to be mewed up, and take only the liberty of going from our chamber to the dining room and from the dining room to our chamber again? And like a bird in a cage with two perches only to hop up and down, up and down?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Well, thou art a mad wench.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Wouldst thou never have us go to a play but with our grave relations? Never take the air but with our grave relations? To feed their pride, and make the world believe it is in their power to afford some gallant or other a good bargain?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: But I am afraid we shall be known again.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Pish! The men were only acquainted with our vizards and our petticoats, and they are wore out long since. How I envy that sex! Well, we cannot plague 'em enough when we have it in our power for those privileges which custom has allowed 'em above us.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: The truth is, they can run and ramble here and there and everywhere, and we poor fools rather think the better of 'em.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: From one playhouse to the other playhouse, and if they like neither the play nor the women they seldom stay any longer than the combing of their periwigs or a whisper or two with a friend. And then they cock their caps and out they strut again.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: But whatsoever we do, prithee now let us resolve to be mighty honest.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: There I agree with thee.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: And if we find the gallants like lawless subjects, who the more their princes grant the more they impudently crave—

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We'll become absolute tyrants, and deprive 'em of all the privileges we gave 'em.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Upon these conditions I am contented to trail a pike under thee. March along, girl.

div2.head: SCENE 1

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Was there ever a couple of fops better matched than these two knights are?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: They are harp and violin. Nature has so tuned 'em as if she intended they should always play the fool in consort.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now is Sir Oliver secure, for he dares not go home 'till he's quite drunk. And then he grows valiant, insults and defies his sweet lady, for which with prayers and tears he's forced to feign a bitter repentance the next morning.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: What do we here idling in the Mulberry Garden? Why do not we make this visit then?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now art thou as mad upon this trail as if we were upon a hot scent.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Since we know the bush, why do we not start the game?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Gently, good Frank. First know that the laws of honor prescribed in such nice cases will not allow me to carry thee along with me. And next, hast thou so little wit to think that a discreet lady that has had the experience of so much humane frailty can have so good an opinion of the constancy of her servant as to lead him into temptation?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Then we must not hope her ladyship should make us acquainted with these gentlewomen.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Thou mayest as reasonably expect that an old rook should bring a young snap acquainted with his bubble. But advantages may be hereafter made by my admission into the family.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: What is to be done then?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why, look you, thus I have contrived it. Sir Oliver, when I began to grow resty, that he might incline me a little more to drunkenness in my ear discovered to me the humor of his dear friend Sir Joslin. He assured me that when he was in that good natured condition, to requite their courtesy, he always carried the good company home with him and recommended them to his kinswomen.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Very good!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now after the fresh air has breathed on us a while, and expelled the vapors of the wine we have drunk, thou shalt return to these two sots whom we left at the French House according to our promise, and tell 'em I am a little stayed by some unlucky business and will be with 'em presently. Thou wilt find 'em tired with long fight, weak and unable to observe their order. Charge 'em briskly and in a moment thou shalt rout 'em, and with little or no damage to thyself gain an absolute victory.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Very well!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: In the meantime I will make my visit to the longing lady, and order my business so handsomely that I will be with thee again immediately to make an experiment of the good humor of Sir Joslin.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Let's about it.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Tis yet too early, we must drill away a little time here that my excuses may be more probable and my persecution more tolerable.

div2.stage: Enter Ariana and Gatty with vizards, and pass nimbly over the stage.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Ha, ha! How wantonly they trip it! There is temptation enough in their very gate to stir up the courage of an old alderman. Prithee let us follow 'em.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I have been so often balked with these vizard masks that I have at least a dozen times forsworn 'em: they are a most certain sign of an ill face or, what is worse, an old acquaintance.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: The truth is nothing but some such weighty reason is able to make women deny themselves the pride they have to be seen.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: The evening's fresh and pleasant, and yet there is but little company.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Our course will be the better, these deer cannot herd. Come, come man, let’s follow!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I find it is a mere folly to swear anything; it does but make the devil the more earnest in his temptation.

div2.stage: Enter women [Ariana and Gatty] again and cross the stage.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Now if these should prove two men of war that are crusing here to watch for prizes.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Would they had courage enough to set upon us. I long to be engaged.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Look, look yonder, I protest they chase us.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Let us bear away then. If they be truly valiant they'll quickly make more sail and board us.

div2.stage: The women [Ariana and Mrs Gatty] go out and go about behind the scenes to the other door.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: 'Sdeath, how fleet they are! Whatsoever faults they have, they cannot be broken-winded.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Sure, by that little mincing step they should be country fillies that have been breathed at course-a-park and barley-break: we shall never reach 'em!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I'll follow directly, do thou turn down the crosswalk and meet 'em.

div2.stage: Enter the Women [Ariana and Gatty], and after 'em Courtall at the lower door, and Freeman at the upper on the contrary side.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: By your leave, ladies—

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I perceive you can make bold enough without it.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Your servant, ladies—

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Or any other Ladies that will give themselves the trouble to entertain you.

p.seg: 'Slife, their tongues are as nimble as their heels.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Can you have so little good nature to dash a couple of bashful young men out of countenance, who came out of pure love to tender you their service?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: 'Twere pity to balk 'em, sister.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Indeed methinks they look as if they never had been slipped before.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Yes faith, we have had many a fair course in this paddock, have been very well fleshed and dare boldly fasten.

div2.stage: They kiss their hands with a little force.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Well, I am not the first unfortunate woman that has been forced to give her hand where she never intends to bestow her heart.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Now, do you think 'tis a bargain already?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Faith, would there were some lusty earnest given for fear we should unluckily break off again.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Are you so wild that you must be hooded thus?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Fye, fye, put off these scandals to all good faces.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: For your reputations’ sake we shall keep 'em on. ‘Slife we should be taken for your relations if we durst shew our faces with you thus publicly.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: And what a shame that would be to a couple of young gallants, methinks you should blush to think on't.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: These were pretty toys, invented first merely for the good of us poor lovers to deceive the jealous and to blind the malicious. But the proper use is so wickedly perverted that it makes all honest men hate the fashion mortally.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: A good face is as seldom covered with a vizard mask as a good hat with an oiled case. And yet on my conscience, you are both handsome.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Do but remove 'em a little, to satisfy a foolish scruple.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: This is a just punishment you have brought upon yourselves by that unpardonable sin of talking.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You can only brag now of your acquaintance with a farendon gown and a piece of black velvet.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: The truth is there are some vain fellows whose loose behavior of late has given great discouragement to the honorable proceedings of all virtuous ladies.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: But I hope you have more charity than to believe us of the number of the wicked.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: There's not a man of you to be trusted.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: What a shame is it to your whole sex that a woman is more fit to be a privy counsellor than a young gallant a lover?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This is a pretty kind of fooling, ladies, for men that are idle. But you must bid a little fairer if you intend to keep us from our serious business.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Truly you seem to be men of great employment, that are every moment rattling from the eating houses to the playhouses, from the playhouses to the Mulberry Garden, that live in a perpetual hurry and have little leisure for such an idle entertainment.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now would not I see thy face for the world. If it should but be half so good as thy humor thou wouldst dangerously tempt me to doat upon thee and, forgetting all shame, become constant.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I perceive by your fooling here that wit and good humor may make a man in love with a blackamoor. That the devil should contrive it so that we should have earnest business now.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Would they would but be so kind to meet us here again tomorrow.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You are full of business, and 'twould but take you off of your employments.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: And we are very unwilling to have the sin to answer for of ruining a couple of such hopeful young men.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Must we then despair?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: The ladies you are going to will not be so hard-hearted.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (to Freeman) On my conscience, they love us and begin to grow jealous already.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Who knows but this may prove the luckier adventure of the two?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, we know you have a mind to meet us. We cannot see you blush, speak it out boldly.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Will you swear, then, not to visit any other women before that time?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Not that we are jealous, but because we would not have you tired with the impertinent conversation of our sex and come to us dull and out of humor.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Invent an oath, and let it be so horrid 'twould make an atheist start to hear it.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: And I will swear it readily, that I will not so much as speak to a woman 'till I speak to you again.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: But are you troubled with that foolish scruple of keeping an oath?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: O most religiously!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: And may we not enlarge our hopes upon a little better acquaintance?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: You see all the freedom we allow.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: It may be we may be entreated to hear a fiddle, or mingle in a country dance, or so.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well! We are in too desperate a condition to stand upon articles and are resolved to yield on any terms.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Be sure you be punctual now!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Will you be sure?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Or else may we become a couple of credulous coxcombs and be jilted ever after. Your servants, ladies.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: I wonder what they think of us!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You may easily imagine, for they are not of a humor so little in fashion to believe the best. I assure you the most favorable opinion they can have is that we are still a little wild and stand in need of better manning.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Prithee, dear girl, what dost think of 'em?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Faith so well, that I'm ashamed to tell thee.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Would I had never seen 'em!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Ha! Is it come to that already?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Prithee, let's walk a turn or two more and talk of 'em.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Let us take care then we are not too particular in their commendations, lest we should discover we entrench upon one another’s inclinations and so grow quarrelsome.

div2.head: SCENE 2

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Dear madam, do not afflict yourself thus unreasonably. I dare lay my life, it is not want of devotion but opportunity that stays him.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Ingrateful man! To be so insensible of a lady’s passion!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: If I thought he were so wicked I should hate him strangely. But, madam—

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Do not speak one word in his behalf, I am resolved to forget him. Perfidious mortal, to abuse so sweet an opportunity!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Hark, here is somebody coming up stairs.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Peace, he may yet redeem his honor.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your humble servant, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: (Starting) Mr Courtall, for heaven’s sake, how came you hither?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Guided by my good fortune, madam. Your servant, Mrs Sentry.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Your humble servant, sir; I protest you made me start too, to see you come in thus unexpectedly.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I did not imagine it could be known I was in town yet.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Sir Oliver did me the favor to make me a visit and dine with me today, which brought me to the knowledge of this happiness, madam. And as soon as I could possibly, I got the freedom to come hither and enjoy it.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You have ever been extreme obliging, sir.

p.seg: 'Tis a worthy gentleman, how punctual he is to my directions!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Will you be pleased to repose, sir? Sentry, set some chairs.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: With much difficulty, madam, I broke out of my company and was forced by the importunity of one Sir Joslin Jolly, I think they call him, to engage my honor I would return again immediately.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You must not so soon rob me of so sweet a satisfaction.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: No consideration, madam, could take me from you but that I know my stay at this time must needs endanger your honor. And how often I have denied myself the greatest satisfaction in the world to keep that unblemished you yourself can witness.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Indeed I have often had great trials of your generosity in those many misfortunes that have attended our innocent affections.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Sir Oliver, madam, before I did perceive it, was got near that pitch of drunkenness which makes him come reeling home and unmanfully insult over your ladyship. And how subject he is then to injure you with an unjust suspicion you have often told me, which makes me careful not to be surprised here.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Repose yourself a little, but a little, dear sir; these virtuous principles make you worthy to be trusted with a lady’s honor. Indeed Sir Oliver has his failings; yet I protest, Mr Courtall, I love him dearly but cannot be altogether unsensible of your generous passion.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (Aside) Aye, aye, I am a very passionate lover! Indeed this escape has only given me leisure to look upon my happiness.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Is my woman retired?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Most dutifully, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Then let me tell you, sir: yet we may make very good use of it.

p.seg: Now am I going to be drawn in again.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: If Sir Oliver be in that indecent condition you speak of, tomorrow he will be very submissive, as it is meet for so great a misdemeanor. Then can I, feigning a desperate discontent, take my own freedom without the least suspicion.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This is very luckily and obligingly thought on, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Now if you will be pleased to make an assignation, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Tomorrow about ten a clock in the lower walk of the New Exchange, out of which we can quickly pop into my coach.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: But I am still so pestered with my woman, I dare not go without her. On my conscience she's very sincere, but it is not good to trust our reputations too much to the frailty of a servant.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I will bring my chariot, madam, that will hold but two.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: O most ingeniously imagined, dear sir! For by that means I shall have a just excuse to give her leave to see a relation, and bid her stay there till I call her.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: It grieves me much to leave you so soon, madam, but I shall comfort myself with the thoughts of the happiness you have made me hope for.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I wish it were in my power eternally to oblige you, dear sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your humble servant, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
Your humble servant, sweet sir. Exit Courtall.
Sentry! Why, Sentry! Where are you?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Here, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: What a strange thing is this! Will you never take warning but still be leaving me alone in these suspicious occasions?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I was but in the next room, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: What may Mr Courtall think of my innocent intentions? I protest, if you serve me so again I shall be strangely angry. You should have more regard to your lady's honor.

p.seg: If I stay in the room she will not speak kindly to me in a week after, and if I go out she always chides me thus. This is a strange infirmity she has, but I must bear with it; for, on my conscience, custom has made it so natural she cannot help it.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Are my cousins come home yet?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Not yet, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Dost thou know whither they went this evening?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I heard them say they would go take the air, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Well, I see it is impossible with virtuous counsel to reclaim them. Truly they are so careless of their own I could wish Sir Joslin would remove 'em for fear they should bring an unjust imputation on my honor.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Heavens forbid, madam!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Your servant, cousins.

sp.speaker: GATTY AND ARIANA
sp.p: Your servant, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: How have you spent the cool of the evening?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: As the custom is, madam, breathing the fresh air in the park and Mulberry Garden.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Without the company of a relation or some discreet body to justify your reputations to the world? You are young and may be yet insensible of it, but this is a strange censorious age, I assure you.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Hark! what music's this?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I'll lay my life my uncle's drunk, and hath picked us up a couple of worthy servants and brought them home with him in triumph.

div2.stage: Enter the Music playing, Sir Oliver strutting and swaggering, Sir Joslin singing and dancing with Mr Courtall and Mr Freeman in each hand. Gatty and Ariana, seeing Courtall and Freeman, shriek and exeunt.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey day! I told you they were a couple of skittish fillies, but I never knew 'em boggle at a man before. I'll fetch 'em again, I warrant you, boys.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: (to Courtall) These are the very self-same gowns and petticoats!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Their surprise confirms us it must be them.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: 'Slife, we have betrayed ourselves very pleasantly.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now am I undone to all intents and purposes, for they will innocently discover all to my lady and she will have no mercy.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: (Strutting) Dan, dan, da ra, dan... Avoid my presence, the very sight of that face makes me more impotent than an eunuch.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Dear Sir Oliver!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Forbear your conjugal clippings, I will have a wench. Thou shalt fetch me a wench, Sentry.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Can you be so inhumane to my dear lady?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Peace, envy, or I will have thee executed for petty treason: thy skin flayed off, stuffed and hung up in my hall in the country as a terror to my whole family.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What crime can deserve this horrid punishment?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I'll tell thee, Ned: 'twas my fortune t'other day to have an intrigue with a tinker's wife in the country, and this malicious slut betrayed the very ditch where we used to make our assignations to my lady.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: She deserves your anger indeed, Sir Oliver. But be not so unkind to your virtuous lady.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Thou dost not know her, Frank. I have had a design to break her heart ever since the first month that I had her, and 'tis so tough that I have not yet cracked one string on't.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You are too unmerciful, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hang her, Ned, by wicked policy she would usurp my empire, and in her heart is a very pharaoh, for every night she's a putting me upon making brick without straw.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I cannot see a virtuous lady so afflicted without offering her some consolation. (Aside to her [Lady Cockwood]) Dear Madam, is it not as I told you?

p.seg: The fates could not have been more propitious, and I shall not be wanting to the furthering of our mutual happiness.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Joslin, with Ariana and Gatty in each hand, dancing and singing.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN

lg.l: This is sly and pretty,
And this is wild and witty;
If either stayed
Till she died a maid,
I’faith 'twould be great pity.

sp.p:
Here they are, boys, i'faith, and now little Joslin's a man of his word. Heuk! Sly-girl and Mad-cap, to 'em, to 'em, to 'em, boys, alou! (Flings 'em to Courtall and Freeman, who kiss their hands.)
What's yonder, your lady in tears, brother Cockwood? Come, come, I'll make up all breaches.

lg.l: And we'll all be merry and frolick.

sp.p: Fye, fye, though man and wife are seldom in good humor alone, there are few want the discretion to dissemble it in company.

div2.stage: Sir Joslin, Sir Oliver, and Lady [Cockwood] stand talking together.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I knew we should surprise you, ladies.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Faith, I thought this conjuring to be but a mere jest till now, and could not believe the astrological rascal had been so skillful.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: How exactly he described 'em, and how punctual he was in his directions to apprehend 'em!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Then you have been with a conjurer, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You cannot blame us, ladies: the loss of our hearts was so considerable that it may well excuse the indirect means we took to find out the pretty thieves that stole 'em.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Did not I tell you what men of business these were, sister?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I vow I innocently believed they had some pre-engagement to a scrivener or a surgeon, and wished 'em so well that I am sorry to find 'em so perfidious.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Why, we have kept our oaths, ladies!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: You are much beholding to providence.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: But we are more, sister. For had we once been deluded into an opinion they had been faithful, who knows into what inconveniences that error might have drawn us?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why should you be so unreasonable, ladies, to expect that from us we should scarce have hoped for from you? Fye, fye, the keeping of one’s word is a thing below the honor of a gentleman.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: A poor shift! Fit only to uphold the reputation of a paltry citizen.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, come, all will be well again, I warrant you, lady.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: These are insupportable injuries, but I will bear 'em with an invincible patience and tomorrow make him dearly sensible how unworthy he has been.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Tomorrow my brother Cockwood will be another man. So, boys, and how do you like the flesh and blood of the Jollies? Heuk, Sly-girl and Mad-cap, hey! Come, come, you have heard them exercise their tongues a while. Now you shall see them ply their feet a little. This is a clean-limbed wench, and has neither spavin, splinter, nor wind gall; tune her a jig, and play't roundly, you shall see her bounce it away like a nimble frigot before a fresh gale. Hey, methinks I see her under sail already.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey, my little Mad-cap... Here's a girl of the true breed of the Jollies, i'faith... But hark you, hark you, a consultation, gentlemen (bear up, brother Cockwood, a little): what think you if we pack these idle housewives to bed now and retire into a room by ourselves, and have a merry catch and a bottle or two of the best, and perfect the good work we have so unanimously carried on today?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: A most admirable intrigue... tan, dan, da, ra, dan. Come, come, march to your several quarters. Go, we have sent for a civil person or two and are resolved to fornicate in private.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: This is a barbarous return of all my kindness.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN AND COURTALL
sp.p: Your humble servant, madam.

div2.stage: Exit Lady Cockwood and Mrs Sentry.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Ariana and Gatty] Hark you, hark you, ladies! Do not harbor too ill an opinion of us, for faith, when you have had a little more experience of the world you'll find we are no such abominable rascals.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We shall be so charitable to think no worse of you than we do of all mankind for your sakes, only that you are perjured, perfidious, inconstant, ungrateful.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Nay, nay, that's enough in all conscience, ladies. And now you are sensible what a shameful thing it is to break one’s word, I hope you'll be more careful to keep yours tomorrow.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: “Invent an oath, and let it be so horrid—”

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Nay, nay, it is too late for raillery, i'faith, ladies.

sp.speaker: GATTY AND ARIANA
sp.p:
Well, your servant then.
Your servant, ladies.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Now the enemy's marched out...

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Then the castle's our own, boys! Hey!

lg.l: And here and there I had her,
And everywhere I had her,
Her toy was such, that every touch
Would make a lover madder.

sp.p: Hey, brave Sir Joslin!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Ah my dear little witty Joslin, let me hug thee.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Strike up, you obstreperous rascals, and march along before us.

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: Mrs Trinket sitting in a shop, people passing by as in the Exchange.

sp.speaker: MRS TRINKET
sp.p:
What d'ye buy? What d'ye lack, gentlemen? Gloves, ribbons, and essences? Ribbons, gloves, and essences? Enter Mr Courtall.
Mr Courtall! I thought you had a quarrel to the Change and were resolved we should never see you here again.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your unkindness, indeed, Mrs Trinket, had been enough to make a man banish himself forever.

sp.speaker: MRS TRINKET
sp.p: Look you, yonder comes fine Mrs Gazette; thither you intended your visit, I am sure.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: Mr Courtall! Your servant.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your servant, Mrs Gazette.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: This happiness was only meant to Mrs Trinket, had it not been my good fortune to pass by, by chance, I should have lost my share on't.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This is too cruel, Mrs Gazette, when all the unkindness is on your side, to rally your servant thus.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: I vow this tedious absence of yours made me believe you intended to try an experiment on my poor heart, to discover that hidden secret: how long a despairing lover may languish without the sight of the party.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You are always very pleasant on this subject, Mrs Gazette.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: And have not you reason to be so too?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Not that I know of.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: Yes, you hear the good news.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What good news?

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: How well this dissembling becomes you! But now I think better on't, it cannot concern you: you are more a gentleman than to have an amour last longer than an Easter term with a country lady. And yet there are some I see as well in the country as in the city that have a pretty way of housewifing a lover, and can spin an intrigue out a great deal farther than others are willing to do.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What pretty art have they, good Mrs Gazette?

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: When tradesmen see themselves in an ill condition, and are afraid of breaking, can they do better than to take in a good substantial partner to help to carry on their trading?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Sure you have been at riddle me, riddle me; lately you are so wondrous witty.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: And yet I believe my Lady Cockwood is so haughty she had rather give over the vanity of an intrigue than take in a couple of young handsome kinswomen to help to maintain it.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I knew it would out at last. Indeed it is the principle of most good women that love gaming, when they begin to grow a little out of play themselves, to make an interest in some young gamester or other in hopes to rook a favor now and then. But you are quite out in your policy: my Lady Cockwood is none of these, I assure you. Hark you, Mrs Gazette, you must needs bestir yourself a little for me this morning, or else heaven have mercy on a poor sinner.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: I hope this wicked woman has no design upon your body already, alas! I pity your tender conscience.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I have always made thee my confident, and now I come to thee as to a faithful counsellor.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: State your case.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why, this ravenous kite is upon wing already, is fetching a little compass, and will be here within this half hour to swoop me away.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: And you would have me your scarecrow?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Something of that there is in’t: she is still your customer.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: I have furnished her and the young ladies with a few fashionable toys since they came to town, to keep 'em in countenance at a play or in the park.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I would have thee go immediately to the young ladies and by some device or other entice 'em hither.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: I came just now from taking measure of 'em for a couple of handkerchiefs.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: How unlucky's this!

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: They were calling for their hoods and scarfs and are coming hither to lay out a little money in ribbons and essences. I have recommended them to Mrs Trinket’s shop here.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This falls out more luckily than what I had contrived myself, or could have done! For here will they be busy just before the door where we have made our appointment. But if this long-winged devil should chance to truss me before they come...

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: I will only step up and give some directions to my maid about a little business that is in haste and come down again and watch her. If you are snapped, I'll be with you presently and rescue you, I warrant you, or at least stay you 'till more company come. She dares not force you away in my sight; she knows I am great with Sir Oliver, and as malicious a devil as the best of 'em. Your servant, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Freeman! 'Tis well you are come.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Well! What counter plot? What hopes of disappointing the old, and of seeing the young ladies? I am ready to receive your orders.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Faith, things are not so well contrived as I could have wished 'em, and yet I hope by the help of Mrs Gazette to keep my word, Frank.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Nay, now I know what tool thou hast made choice of, I make no question but the business will go well forward. But I am afraid this last unlucky business has so distasted these young trouts they will not be so easily tickled as they might have been.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Never fear it: whatsoever women say, I am sure they seldom think the worse of a man for running at all; 'tis a sign of youth and high metal, and makes them rather piquée who shall tame him. That which troubles me most is we lost the hopes of variety, and a single intrigue in love is as dull as a single plot in a play, and will tire a lover worse than t'other does an audience.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: We cannot be long without some under-plots in this town. Let this be our main design, and if we are anything fortunate in our contrivance we shall make it a pleasant comedy.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
Leave all things to me and hope the best. Be gone, for I expect their coming immediately. Walk a turn or two above, or fool a while with pretty Mrs Anvil, and scent your eyebrows and periwig with a little essence of oranges or jessamine. And when you see us all together at Mrs Gazette’s shop put in as it were by chance. I protest yonder comes the old haggard, to your post quickly. ‘Sdeath, where's Gazette and these young ladies now? Exit Freeman. Enter Lady Cockwood and Mrs Sentry.
O Madam, I have waited here at least an hour, and time seems very tedious when it delays so great a happiness as you bring with you.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I vow, sir, I did but stay to give Sir Oliver his due correction for those unseemly injuries he did me last night. Is your coach ready?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Yes, madam, but how will you dispose of your maid?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: My maid! For heaven’s sake, what do you mean, sir? Do I ever use to go abroad without her?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Tis upon no design, madam, I speak it, I assure you. But my glass coach broke last night and I was forced to bring my chariot, which can hold but two.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: O heaven! You must excuse me, dear sir, for I shall deny myself the sweetest recreations in the world rather than yield to anything that may bring a blemish upon my spotless honor.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: Your humble servant, madam. Your servant, Mr Courtall.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD AND COURTALL
sp.p: Your servant, Mrs Gazette.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: I am extreme glad to see your ladyship here: I intended to send my maid to your lodgings this afternoon, madam, to tell you I have a parcel of new lace come in, the prettiest patterns that ever were seen. For I am very desirous so good a customer as your ladyship should see 'em first and have your choice.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I am much beholding to you, Mrs Gazette; I was newly come into the Exchange and intended to call at your shop before I went home.

div2.stage: Enter Ariana and Gatty, Mrs Gazette goes to 'em.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Sdeath, here are your cousins too! now there is no hope left for a poor unfortunate lover to comfort himself withal.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Will fate never be more propitious?

sp.speaker: GATTY AND ARIANA
sp.p: Your servant, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I am newly come into the Exchange and by chance met with Mr Courtall here, who will needs give himself the trouble to play the gallant and wait upon me.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Does your ladyship come to buy?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: A few trifles. Mrs Gazette says she has a parcel of very fine new laces, shall we go look upon 'em?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: We will only fancy a suit of knots or two at this shop, and buy a little essence, and wait upon your ladyship immediately.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Mrs Gazette, you are skilled in the fashion, pray let our choice have your approbation.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: Most gladly, madam.

div2.stage: All go to the shop to look upon ware but Courtall and Lady Cockwood.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Sdeath, madam, if you had made no ceremony but stepped into the coach presently we had escaped this mischief.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: My over-tenderness of my honor has blasted all my hopes of happiness.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: To be thus unluckily surprised in the height of all our expectation leaves me no patience.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Moderate your passion a little, sir, I may yet find out a way.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Oh 'tis impossible, madam, never think on't now you have been seen with me: to leave 'em upon any pretense will be so suspicious that my concern for your honor will make me so feverish and disordered that I shall lose the taste of all the happiness you give me.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Methinks you are too scrupulous, heroic sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Besides the concerns I have for you, madam, you know the obligations I have to Sir Oliver, and what professions of friendship there are on both sides. And to be thought perfidious and ungrateful, what an affliction would that be to a generous spirit!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Must we then unfortunately part thus?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now I have better thought on't, that is not absolutely necessary neither.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: These words revive my dying joys, dear sir, go on.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I will by and by, when I see it most convenient, beg the favor of your ladyship and your young kinswomen to accept of a treat and a fiddle. You make some little difficulty at first, but upon earnest persuasion comply and use your interest to make the young ladies do so too. Your company will secure their reputations, and their company take off from you all suspicion.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: The natural inclination they have to be jigging will make them very ready to comply. But what advantage can this be to our happiness, dear sir?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why first, madam, if the young ladies or Mrs Gazette have any doubts upon their surprising us together, our joining company will clear 'em all. Next, we shall have some satisfaction in being an afternoon together, though we enjoy not that full freedom we so passionately desire.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Very good, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: But then lastly, madam, we gain an opportunity to contrive another appointment tomorrow, which may restore us unto all those joys we have been so unfortunately disappointed of today.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: This is a very prevailing argument indeed. But since Sir Oliver believes I have conceived so desperate a sorrow 'tis fit we should keep this from his knowledge.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Are the young ladies secret?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: They have the good principles not to betray themselves, I assure you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Then 'tis but going to a house that is not haunted by the company and we are secure. And, now I think on't, the Bear in Drury Lane is the fittest place for our purpose.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
I know your honor, dear sir, and submit to your discretion.
[To Ariana and Gatty] Have you gratified your fancies, cousins?

div2.stage: To them Ariana, Gatty, and Mrs Gazette from the shop.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: We are ready to wait upon you, madam.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I never saw colors better mingled.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: How lively they set off one another, and how they add to the complexion!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Mr Courtall, your most humble servant.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Pray, madam, let me have the honor to wait upon you and these young ladies till I see you in your coach.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Your friendship to Sir Oliver would engage you in an unnecessary trouble.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Let not an idle ceremony take you from your serious business, good sir.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I should rather have expected to have seen you, sir, walking in Westminster Hall, watching to make a match at tennis or waiting to dine with a Parliament man than to meet you in such an idle place as the Exchange is.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Methinks, ladies, you are well acquainted with me upon the first visit.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: We received your character before. You know, sir, in the Mulberry Garden upon oath.

p.seg: 'Sdeath, what shall I do? Now out comes all my roguery.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Yet I am apt to believe, sister, that was some malicious fellow that willfully perjured himself on purpose to make us have an ill opinion of this worthy gentleman.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Some rash men would be apt enough to inquire him out and cut his throat, ladies, but I heartily forgive him whosoever he was. For, on my conscience, 'twas not so much out of malice to me as out of love to you he did it.

sp.speaker: MRS GAZETTE
sp.p: He might imagine Mr Courtall was his rival.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Very likely, Mrs Gazette.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Whosoever he was he was an unworthy fellow, I warrant him: Mr Courtall is known to be a person of worth and honor.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: We took him for an idle fellow, madam, and gave but very little credit to what he said.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Twas very obliging, lady, to believe nothing to the disadvantage of a stranger. [Aside] What a couple of young devils are these?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Since you are willing to give yourself this trouble.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I ought to do my duty, madam.

div2.stage: Exeunt all but Ariana and Gatty.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: How he blushed, and hung down his head!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: A little more had put him as much out of countenance as a country clown is when he ventures to complement his attorney’s daughter.

div2.head: SCENE 2
div2.stage: Enter Sir Joslin and servant [Thomas] severally.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: How now, old boy! Where's my brother Cockwood today?

sp.speaker: THOMAS
sp.p: He desires to be in private, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Why? What's the matter, man?

sp.speaker: THOMAS
sp.p: This is a day of humiliation, sir, with him for last night’s transgression.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: I have business of consequence to impart to him, and must and will speak with him. So, ho! Brother Cockwood!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: (Without) Who's that, my brother Jolly?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: The same, the same! Come away, boy.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: (Without) For some secret reasons I desire to be in private, brother.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: I have such a design on foot as would draw Diogenes out of his tub to follow it. Therefore I say: come away, come away.

div2.stage: Sir Oliver entering in a night gown and slippers.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: There is such a strange temptation in thy voice, never stir.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: What, in thy gown and slippers yet! Why, brother, I have bespoke dinner and engaged Mr Rake-hell, the little smart gentleman I have often promised thee to make thee acquainted withal, to bring a whole bevy of damsels in sky, and pink, and flame-colored taffetas. Come, come, dress thee quickly, there's to be Madam Rampant, a girl that shines and will drink at such a rate she's a mistress for Alexander were he alive again.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: How unluckily this falls out! Thomas, what clothes have I to put on?

sp.speaker: THOMAS
sp.p: None but your penitential suit, sir. All the rest are secured.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Oh, unspeakable misfortune! That I should be in disgrace with my lady now!

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, come, never talk of clothes, put on anything, thou hast a person and a mine will bear it out bravely.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Nay, I know my behavior will show I am a gentleman, but yet the ladies will look scurvily upon me, brother.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: That's a jest, i'faith! He that has terra firma in the country may appear in anything before 'em.

lg.l: For he that would have a wench kind
Ne'er smugs up himself like a ninny,
But plainly tells her his mind
And tickles her first with a guinea.

sp.p: Hey, boy—

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I vow thou hast such a bewitching way with thee!

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: How lovely will the ladies look when they have a beer glass in their hands!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I now have a huge mind to venture. But if this should come to my lady's knowledge...

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: I have bespoke dinner at the Bear, the privatest place in town. There will be no spies to betray us if Thomas be but secret, I dare warrant thee, brother Cockwood.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I have always found Thomas very faithful. But faith, 'tis too unkind considering how tenderly my lady loves me.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Fye, fye, a man and kept so much under correction by a busk and a fan!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Nay, I am in my nature as valiant as any man when once I set out. But, i'faith, I cannot but think how my dear lady will be concerned when she comes home and misses me.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: A pox upon these qualms.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, thou hast seduced me. But I shall look so untowardly...

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Again art thou at it? In, in, and make all the haste that may be, Rake-hell and the ladies will be there before us else.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, thou art an errant devil... Hey for the ladies, brother Jolly!

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey for the ladies, brother Cockwood!

div2.stage: Exit singing “For he that would etc.”

div2.head: SCENE 3

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (Without) Ho, Francis, Humphrey! Show a room there!

div2.stage: Enter Courtall, Freeman, Lady Cockwood, Ariana, Gatty and Mrs Sentry.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Pray, madam, be not so full of apprehension, there is no fear that this should come to Sir Oliver's knowledge.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I were ruined if it should, sir! Dear, how I tremble! I never was in one of these houses before.

p.seg: This is a bait for the young ladies to swallow: she has been in most of the eating houses about town, to my knowledge.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Oh Francis!

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: Your worship’s welcome, sir. But I must needs desire you to walk into the next room, for this is bespoke.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Mr Courtall, did not you say this place was private?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I warrant you, madam. What company dines here, Francis?

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: A couple of country knights: Sir Joslin Jolly and Sir Oliver Cockwood, very honest gentlemen.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Combination to undo me!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Lady Cockwood] Peace, madam, or you'll betray yourself to the waiter!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I am distracted! Sentry, did not I command thee to secure all Sir Oliver's clothes and leave nothing for him to put on but his penitential suit that I might be sure he could not stir abroad today?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I obeyed you in everything, madam, but I have often told you this Sir Joslin is a wicked seducer.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: If my uncle sees us, sister, what will he think of us?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We come but to wait upon her ladyship.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You need not fear, you chickens are secure under the wings of that old hen.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Is there to be nobody, Francis, but Sir Oliver and Sir Joslin?

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: Faith, sir, I was enjoined secrecy, but you have an absolute power over me. Coming lately out of the country where there is but little variety, they have a design to solace themselves with a fresh girl or two, as I understand the business.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh Sentry! Sir Oliver disloyal! My misfortunes come too thick upon me.

p.seg: Now is she afraid of being disappointed on all hands.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I know not what to do, Mr Courtall; I would not be surprised here myself and yet I would prevent Sir Oliver from prosecuting his wicked and perfidious intentions.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: [To Gatty] Now shall we have admirable sport, what with her fear and jealousy.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: [To Ariana] I lay my life she routs the wenches.

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: I must needs desire you to step into the next room, Sir Joslin and Sir Oliver are below already.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I have not power to move a foot.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: We will consider what is to be done within, madam.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Pray, madam, come. I have a design in my head which shall secure you, surprise Sir Oliver and free you from all your fears.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: It cannot be, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Never fear it. Francis, you may own Mr Freeman and I are in the house if they ask for us, but not a word of these ladies as you tender the wearing of your ears.

div2.stage: Enter Sir Joslin, Sir Oliver, and Waiter.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, brother Cockwood, prithee be brisk.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I shall disgrace myself forever, brother.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Pox upon care, never droop like a cock in moulting time, thou art spark enough in all conscience.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: But my heart begins to fail me when I think of my lady.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: What, more qualms yet?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, I will be courageous. But it is not necessary these strangers should know this is my penitential suit, brother.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: They shall not, they shall not. Hark you, old boy, is the meat provided? Is the wine and ice come? And are the melodious rascals at hand I spoke for?

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: Everything will be in a readiness, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: If Mr Rake-hell, with a coach full or two of vizard masks and silk petticoats, call at the door usher 'em up to the place of execution.

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: You shall be obeyed, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Ho, here's my little Rake-hell come! Brother Cockwood, let me commend this ingenious gentleman to your acquaintance. He is a knight of the industry, has many admirable qualities, I assure you.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I am very glad, sir, of this opportunity to know you.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: I am happy, sir, if you esteem me your servant. Hark you, Sir Joslin, is this Sir Oliver Cockwood in earnest?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: In very good earnest I assure you. He is a little fantastical now and then, and dresses himself up in an odd fashion, but that's all one among friends, my little Rake-hell.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Where are the damsels you talked of, brother Jolly? I hope Mr Rake-hell has not forgot 'em.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: They are arming for the ran-counter.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: What, tricking and trimming?

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Even so, and will be here immediately.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: They need not make themselves so full of temptation, my brother Jolly and I can be wicked enough without it.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: The truth is, my little Rake-hell, we are both mighty men at arms, and thou shalt see us charge anon to the terror of the ladies.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Methinks that dress, Sir Oliver, is a little too rustical for a man of your capacity.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I have an odd humor, sir, now and then. But I have wherewithal at home to be as spruce as any man.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Your periwig is too scandalous, Sir Oliver; your black cap and border is never worn but by a fiddler or a waiter.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Prithee, my little Rake-hell, do not put my brother Cockwood out of conceit of himself! Methinks your calot is a pretty ornament, and makes a man look both polite and politic.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: I will allow you 'tis a grave ware, and fit for men of business that are every moment bending of their brows and scratching of their heads, every project would claw out another periwig. But a lover had better appear before his mistress with a bald pate: 'twill make the ladies apprehend a savor, stop their noses and avoid you. 'Slife, love in a cap is more ridiculous than love in a tub or love in a pipkin.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I must confess your whole head is now in fashion, but there was a time when your calot was not so despicable.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Here's a perruque, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: A very good one.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: A very good one? ’Tis the best in England! Pray, Sir Joslin, take him in your hand and draw a comb through him, there is not such another frizz in Europe.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: 'Tis a very fine one indeed.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Pray, Sir Oliver, do me the favor to grace it on your head a little.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: To oblige you, sir.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: You never wore anything became you half so well in all your life before.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Why, you never saw him in your life before.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: That's all one, sir, I know 'tis impossible. Here's a beaver, Sir Oliver, feel him. For fineness, substance, and for fashion, the court of France never saw a better. I have bred him but a fortnight and have him at command already. Clap him on boldly, never hat took the fore-cock and the hind-cock at one motion so naturally.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I think you have a mind to make a spark of me before I see the ladies.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Now you have the mien of a true cavalier, And with one look may make a lady kind, and a Hector humble: and since I named a Hector, here's a sword, sir: sa, sa, sa, try him, Sir Joslin, put him to't, cut through the staple, run him through the door, beat him to the hilts, if he breaks, you shall have liberty to break my pate, And pay me never a groat of the ten for't.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: 'Tis a very pretty weapon indeed, sir.
