sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: The hilt is true French-wrought, and dorée by the best workman in France. This sword and this castor, with an embroidered button and loop which I have to vary him upon occasion, were sent me out of France for a token by my elder brother that went over with a handsome equipage to take the pleasure of this champagne.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Have you a mind to sell these things, sir?

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: That is below a gentleman... yet if a person of honor or a particular friend, such as I esteem you, Sir Oliver, take at any time a fancy to a band, a cravat, a velvet coat, a vest, a ring, a flajolet, or any other little toy I have about me I am good natured and may be easily persuaded to play the fool upon good terms.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Worthy Mr Freeman!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Honest Frank, how cam'st thou to find us out, man?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: By mere chance, sir. Ned Courtall is without writing a letter, and I came in to know whether you had any particular engagements, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: We resolved to be in private. But you are men without exception.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Methinks you intended to be in private indeed, Sir Oliver. 'Sdeath, what disguise have you got on? Are you grown grave since last night and come to sin incognito?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hark you in your ear, Frank, this is my habit of humiliation which I always put on the next day after I have transgressed the better to make my pacification with my incensed lady.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Mr Freeman, your most humble servant, sir.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Oh, my little dapper officer! Are you here?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Ha, Mr Freeman, we have bespoke all the jovial entertainment that a merry wag can wish for: good meat, good wine, and a wholesome wench or two. For the digestion we shall have Madam Rampant, the glory of the town, the brightest she that shines, or else my little Rake-hell is not a man of his word, sir.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: I warrant you she comes, Sir Joslin.

lg.l: (Sings) And if she comes she shall not escape,
If twenty pounds will win her.
Her very eye commits a rape,
’Tis such a tempting sinner.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Well said, Sir Joslin, I see you hold up still and bate not an ace of your good humor.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Noble Mr Courtall!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Bless me, Sir Oliver, what are you going to act a droll? How the people would throng about you if you were but mounted on a few deal-boards in Covent Garden now!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hark you, Ned, this is the badge of my lady's indignation for my last night's offence. Do not insult over a poor sober man in affliction.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, send home for your clothes. I hear you are to have ladies, and you are not to learn at these years how absolutely necessary a rich vest and a perruque are to a man that aims at their favors.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: A pox on't, Ned, my lady's gone abroad in a damned jealous melancholy humor and has commanded her woman to secure 'em.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Under lock and key?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Aye, aye, man. ’Tis usual in these cases, out of pure love in hopes to reclaim me, and to keep me from doing my self an injury by drinking two days together.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What a loving lady 'tis!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: There are sots that would think themselves happy in such a lady, Ned, but to a true bred gentleman all lawful solace is abomination.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Mr Courtall, your most humble servant, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Oh! My little knight of the industry, I am glad to see you in such good company.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: [To Courtall] Courtall, hark you, are the masking habits which you sent to borrow at the playhouse come yet?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Freeman] Yes, and the ladies are almost dressed. This design will add much to our mirth, and give us the benefit of their meat, wine, and music for our entertainment.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: 'Twas luckily thought of.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hark, the music comes.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey, boys! Let 'em enter, let 'em enter!

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: An't please your worships, there is a mask of ladies without that desire to have the freedom to come in and dance.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey, boys!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Did you bid 'em come 'en masquerade, Mr Rake-hell?

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: No. But Rampant is a mad wench, she was half a dozen times a mumming in private company last Shrovetide, and I lay my life she has put 'em all upon this frolic.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: They are mettled girls, I warrant them, Sir Joslin, let 'em be what they will.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Let 'em enter, let 'em enter! Ha, boys!

div2.stage: Enter Music and the ladies in an antic, and then they take out my Lady Cockwood [with] Sir Oliver, the young ladies [Ariana and Gatty with] Courtall and Freeman, and Sentry [with] Sir Joslin, and dance a set dance.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Oh, my little rogue! Have I got thee? How I will turn and wind, and feague thy body!

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Mettle on all sides, mettle on all sides, i'faith. How swimmingly would this pretty little ambling filly carry a man of my body!

lg.l: She's so bonny and brisk,
How she'd carvet and frisk,
If a man were once mounted upon her!
Let me have but a leap
Where 'tis wholesome and cheap,
And a fig for your person of honor.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: 'Tis true, little Joslin, i'faith!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: They have warmed us, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Now am I as rampant as a lion, Ned, and could love as vigorously as a seaman that is newly landed after an East India voyage.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Take my advice, Sir Oliver, do not in your rage deprive yourself of your only hope of an accommodation with your lady.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I had rather have a perpetual civil war than purchase peace at such a dishonorable rate. A poor fiddler after he has been three days persecuted at a country wedding takes more delight in scraping upon his old squeaking fiddle than I do in fumbling on that domestic instrument of mine.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Be not so bitter, Sir Oliver, on your own dear lady.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I was married to her when I was young, Ned, with a design to be baulked as they tie whelps to the bellwether. Where I have been so butted, 'twere enough to fright me were I not pure mettle from ever running at sheep again.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: That's no sure rule, Sir Oliver. For a wife's a dish, of which if a man once surfeit, he shall have a better stomach to all others ever after.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: What a shape is here, Ned! So exact and tempting, 'twould persuade a man to be an implicit sinner and take her face upon credit.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, brother Cockwood, let us get 'em to lay aside these masking fopperies and then we'll feague 'em in earnest. Give us a bottle, waiter.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Not before dinner, good Sir Joslin...

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Lady, though I have out of drollery put myself into this contemptible dress at present, I am a gentleman and a man of courage, as you shall find anon by my brisk behavior.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Sir Joslin! Sir Oliver! These are none of our ladies! They are just come to the door in a coach and have sent for me down to wait upon 'em up to you.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey, boys! More game, more game! Fetch 'em up, fetch 'em up!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Why, what a day of sport will here be, Ned?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: They shall all have fair play, boys.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: And we will match ourselves and make a prize on’t: Ned Courtall and I against Frank Freeman and you brother Jolly, and Rake-hell shall be judge for gloves and silk stockings to be bestowed as the conqueror shall fancy.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Agreed, agreed, agreed!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN AND COURTALL
sp.p: A match, a match!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hey, boys!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: (Sentry pulling off her mask) Oh heavens! My dear lady! Help, help!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: What's here? Sentry and my lady! 'Sdeath, what a condition am I in now, Brother Jolly! You have brought me into this premunire! For heaven’s sake, run down quickly and send the rogue and whores away! Help, help! Oh, help! Dear madam, sweet lady!

div2.stage: Exit Sir Joslin, Sir Oliver kneels down by her [Lady Cockwood].

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Oh she's gone, she's gone!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Give her more air!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Fetch a glass of cold water, Freeman!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Dear madam speak, sweet madam speak!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Out upon thee for a vile hypocrite! Thou art the wicked author of all this! Who but such a reprobate, such an obdurate sinner as thou art, could go about to abuse so sweet a lady?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Dear Sentry, do not stab me with thy words but stab me with thy bodkin rather, that I may here die a sacrifice at her feet for all my disloyal actions.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: No, live, live to be a reproach and a shame to all rebellious husbands. Ah, that she had but my heart! But thou hast bewitched her affections; thou shouldst then dearly smart for this abominable treason.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: So, now she begins to come to herself.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Set her more upright and bend her a little forward.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Unfortunate woman! Let me go! Why do you hold me? Would I had a dagger at my heart, to punish it for loving that ungrateful man.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Dear madam, were I but worthy of your pity and belief.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Peace, peace, perfidious man, I am too tame and foolish! Were I every day at the plays, the park and Mulberry Garden with a kind look secretly to indulge the unlawful passion of some young gallant... or did I associate myself with the gaming madams and were every afternoon at my Lady Brief’s and my Lady Meanwell’s at Umbre and Quebas, pretending ill luck to borrow money of a friend and then pretending good luck to excuse the plenty to a husband, my suspicious demeanor had deserved this. But I, who out of a scrupulous tenderness to my honor and to comply with thy base jealousy, have denied myself all those blameless recreations which a virtuous lady might enjoy, to be thus inhumanely reviled in my own person and thus unreasonably robbed and abused in thine too!

p.seg: Sure she will take up anon, or crack her mind, or else the devil's in’t.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Do not stay and torment me with thy sight! Go, graceless wretch, follow thy treacherous resolutions, do and waste that poor stock of comfort which I should have at home upon those your ravenous cormorants below. I feel my passion begin to swell again.

div2.stage: She has a little fit again.

p.seg: Now will she get an absolute dominion over him, and all this will be my plague in the end!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: (Running up and down) Ned Courtall, Frank Freeman, cousin Ariana, and dear cousin Gatty, for heaven’s sake join all and moderate her passion! Ah, Sentry! Forbear thy unjust reproaches, take pity on thy master! Thou hast a great influence over her, and I have always been mindful of thy favors.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: You do not deserve the least compassion, nor would I speak a good word for you but that I know for all this 'twill be acceptable to my poor lady. Dear madam, do but look up a little, Sir Oliver lies at your feet an humble penitent.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: How bitterly he weeps! How sadly he sighs!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I dare say he counterfeited his sin and is real in his repentance.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Compose yourself a little, pray, madam. All this was mere raillery, a way of talk which Sir Oliver, being well bred, has learned among the gay people of the town.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: If you did but know, madam, what an odious thing it is to be thought to love a wife in good company you would easily forgive him.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: No, no, 'twas the mild correction which I gave him for his insolent behavior last night that has encouraged him again thus to insult over my affections.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, Sir Oliver, out with your bosom secret and clear all things to your lady. Is it not as we have said?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Or may I never have the happiness to be in her good grace again! And as for the harlots, dear madam, here is Ned Courtall and Frank Freeman that have often seen me in company of the wicked. Let 'em speak if they ever knew me tempted to a disloyal action in their lives.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: On my conscience, Madam, I may more safely swear that Sir Oliver has been constant to your ladyship than that a girl of twelve years old has her maidenhead this warm and ripening age.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Here's my brother Jolly too can witness the loyalty of my heart, and that I did not intend any treasonable practice against your ladyship in the least.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Unless feaguing 'em with a beer glass be included in the statute. Come, Mr Courtall, to satisfy my lady and put her in a little good humor, let us sing the catch I taught you yesterday that was made by a country vicar on my brother Cockwood and me.

lg.l: (They sing.) Love and wenching are toys
Fit to please beardless boys,
Th'are sports we hate worse than a leaguer,
When we visit a miss
We still brag how we kiss
But 'tis with a bottle we feague her.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, come, madam, let all things be forgot. Dinner is ready, the cloth is laid in the next room, let us in and be merry. There was no harm meant as I am true little Joslin.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Sir Oliver knows I can't be angry with him, though he plays the naughty man thus. But why, my dear, would y'expose yourself in this ridiculous habit to the censure of both our honors?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Indeed I was to blame to be over-persuaded. I intended dutifully to retire into the pantry, and there civilly to divert myself at backgammon with the butler.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Faith, I must even own the fault was mine, I enticed him hither, lady.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: [To Courtall] How the devil, Ned, came they to find us out here?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Sir Oliver] No bloodhound draws so sure as a jealous woman.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: [To Courtall] I am afraid Thomas has been unfaithful. Prithee, Ned, speak to my lady that there may be a perfect understanding between us, and that Sentry may be sent home for my clothes that I may no longer wear the marks of her displeasure.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
[To Sir Oliver] Let me alone, Sir Oliver. (He goes to my Lady Cockwood.)
How do you find yourself, madam, after this violent passion?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: This has been a lucky adventure, Mr Courtall. Now am I absolute mistress of my own conduct for a time.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Then shall I be a happy man, madam. I knew this would be the consequence of all, and yet could not I forbear the project.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: (To Sir Joslin) How didst thou shuffle away Rake-hell and the lady's brother?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: [To Sir Oliver] I have appointed 'em to meet us at six o’clock at the new Spring Garden.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: [To Sir Joslin] Then will we yet, in spite of the stars that have crossed us, be in conjunction with Madam Rampant, brother.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, gentlemen, dinner is on the table.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Ha! Sly-girl and Mad-cap, I'll enter you, i'faith! Since you have found the way to the Bear, I'll feague you.

lg.l: When we visit a miss
We still brag how we kiss,
But 'tis with a bottle we feague her.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
A lady cannot be too jealous of her servants love this faithless and inconstant age. His amorous carriage to that prating girl today, though he pretends it was to blind Sir Oliver, I fear will prove a certain sign of his revolted heart. The letters I have counterfeited in these girls’ name will clear all: if he accept of that appointment and refuses mine I need not any longer doubt. (Enter Sentry).
Sentry, have the letters and message been delivered as I directed?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Punctually, madam. I knew they were to be found at the latter end of a play. I sent a porter first with the letter to Mr Courtall, who was at the King’s House; he sent for him out by the doorkeeper and delivered it into his own hands.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Did you keep on your vizard, that the fellow might not know how to describe you?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I did, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: And how did he receive it?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Like a traitor to all goodness, with all the signs of joy imaginable.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Be not angry, Sentry, 'tis as my heart wished it. What did you do with the letter to Mr Freeman? For I thought fit to deceive 'em both, to make my policy less suspicious to Courtall.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: The porter found him at the Duke’s House, madam, and delivered it with like care.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: After the letters were delivered, madam, I went myself to the playhouse and sent in for Mr Courtall, who came out to me immediately. I told him your ladyship presented your humble service to him, and that Sir Oliver was going into the city with Sir Joslin to visit his brother Cockwood, and that it would add much more to your ladyship’s happiness if he would be pleased to meet you in Grays Inn walks this lovely evening.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: And how did he entertain the motion?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Bless me, I tremble still to think upon it! I could not have imagined he had been so wicked. He counterfeited the greatest passion, railed at his fate, and swore a thousand horrid oaths that since he came into the playhouse he had notice of a business that concerned both his honor and fortune and that he was an undone man if he did not go about it presently. Prayed me to desire your ladyship to excuse him this evening and that tomorrow he would be wholly at your devotion.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha! He little thinks how much he has obliged me.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I had much ado to forbear upbraiding him with his ingratitude to your ladyship.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Poor Sentry! be not concerned for me, I have conquered my affection and thou shalt find it is not jealousy has been my councilor in this. Go, let our hoods and masks be ready that I may surprise Courtall and make the best advantage of this lucky opportunity.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I obey you, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: How am I filled with indignation! To find my person and my passion both despised, and, what is more, so much precious time fooled away in fruitless expectation. I would poison my face so I might be revenged on this ingrateful villain.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: My dearest!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: My dearest dear! Prithee do not go into the city tonight.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: My brother Jolly is gone before, and I am to call him at Counsellor Trott's chamber in the Temple.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Well, if you did but know the fear I have upon me when you are absent you would not seek occasions to be from me thus.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Let me comfort thee with a kiss. What should'st thou be afraid of?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I cannot but believe that every woman that sees thee must be in love with thee as I am. Do not blame my jealousy.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I protest I would refuse a countess rather than abuse thee, poor heart.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: And then you are so desperate upon the least occasion, I should have acquainted you else with something that concerns your honor.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: My honor! You ought in duty to do it.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Nay, I knew how passionate you would be presently; therefore you shall never know it.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Do not leave me in doubt, I shall suspect everyone I look upon. I will kill a common councilman or two before I come back if you do not tell me.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Dear, how I tremble! Will you promise me you will not quarrel then? If you tender my life and happiness, I am sure you will not.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I will bear anything rather than be an enemy to thy quiet, my dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I could wish Mr Courtall a man of better principles, because I know you love him, my dear.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Why, what has he done?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I always treated him with great respects out of my regard to your friendship. But he, like an impudent man as he is, today misconstruing my civility in most unseemly language made a foul attempt upon my honor.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Death, and hell, and furies, I will have my pumps and longsword!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh, I shall faint! Did not you promise me you would not be so rash?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, I will not kill him for fear of murdering thee, my dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You may decline your friendship, and by your coldness give him no encouragement to visit our family.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I think thy advice the best for this once, indeed, for it is not fit to publish such a business. But if he should be ever tempting or attempting let me know it, prithee, my dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: If you moderate yourself according to my directions now, I shall never conceal anything from you, that may increase your just opinion of my conjugal fidelity.

p.seg: Was ever man blessed with such a virtuous lady! Yet cannot I forbear going a ranging again. Now must I to the Spring Garden to meet my brother Jolly and Madam Rampant.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Prithee, be so good to think how melancholy I spend my time here. For I have joy in no company but thine, and let that bring thee home a little sooner.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Thou hast been so kind in this discovery, that I am loath to leave thee.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I wish you had not been engaged so far.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Aye, that's it. Farewell, my virtuous dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
Farewell, my dearest dear. I know he has not courage enough to question Courtall. But this will make him hate him, increase his confidence of me, and justify my banishing that false fellow from our house. It is not fit a man that has abused my love should come hither and pry into my actions. Besides, this will make his access more difficult to that wanton baggage. Enter Ariana and Gatty with their hoods and masks.
Whither are you going, cousins?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: To take the air upon the water, madam.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: And for variety, to walk a turn or two in the new Spring Garden.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I heard you were gone abroad with Mr Courtall and Mr Freeman.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: For heaven's sake, why should your ladyship have such an ill opinion of us?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: The truth is, before I saw you, I believed it merely the vanity of that prating man. Mr Courtall told Mrs Gazette this morning that you were so well acquainted already that you would meet him and Mr Freeman anywhere, and that you had promised 'em to receive and make appointment by letters.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Oh, impudent man!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Now you see the consequence, sister, of our rambling: they have raised this false story from our innocent fooling with 'em in the Mulberry Garden last night.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I could almost foreswear ever speaking to a man again.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Was Mr Courtall in the Mulberry Garden last night?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Yes, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: And did he speak to you?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: There passed a little harmless raillery betwixt us. But you amaze me, madam.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: I could not imagine any man could be thus unworthy.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: He has quite lost my good opinion too. In duty to Sir Oliver, I have hitherto showed him some countenance, but I shall hate him hereafter for your sakes. But I detain you from your recreations, cousins.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We are very much obliged to your ladyship for this timely notice.

sp.speaker: GATTY AND ARIANA
sp.p: Your servant, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Your servant, cousins... In the Mulberry Garden last night! When I sat languishing and vainly expecting him at home! This has incensed me so that I could kill him. I am glad these girls are gone to the Spring Garden, it helps my design: the letters I have counterfeited have appointed Courtall and Freeman to meet them there. They will produce 'em and confirm all I have said. I will daily poison these girls with such lies as shall make their quarrel to Courtall irreconcilable, and render Freeman only suspected. For I would not have him thought equally guilty: he secretly began to make an address to meet the at Bear, and this breach shall give him an opportunity to pursue it.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Here are your things, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: That's well. Oh, Sentry! I shall once more be happy, for now Mr Courtall has given me an occasion that I may without ingratitude check his unlawful passion and free myself from the trouble of an intrigue that gives me every day such fearful apprehensions of my honor.

div2.head: SCENE 2
div2.stage: Enter Sir Joslin, Rake-hell, and Waiter.

sp.speaker: WAITER
sp.p: Will you be pleased to walk into an arbor, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: By and by, good sir.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: I wonder why Sir Oliver is not come yet.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Nay, he will not fail, I warrant thee, boy. But what's the matter with thy nose, my little Rake-hell?

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: A foolish accident. Jesting at the Fleece this afternoon I mistook my man a little, a dull rogue that could not understand raillery, made a sudden repartee with a quart-pot, Sir Joslin.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Why didst not thou stick him to the wall, my little Rake-hell?

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: The truth is, Sir Joslin, he deserved it. But look you, in case of a doubtful wound I am unwilling to give my friends too often the trouble to bail me. And if it should be mortal, you know a younger brother has not wherewithal to rebate the edge of a witness and mollify the hearts of a jury.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: This is very prudently considered indeed.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: 'Tis time to be wise, sir. My courage has almost run me out of a considerable annuity. When I lived first about this town, I agreed with a surgeon for twenty pounds a quarter to cure me of all the knocks, bruises, and green wounds I should receive, and in one half year the poor fellow begged me to be released of his bargain and swore I would undo him else in lint and balsam.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Ho! Here's my brother Cockwood come!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Aye, brother Jolly, I have kept my word, you see. But 'tis a barbarous thing to abuse my lady, I have had such a proof of her virtue, I will tell thee all anon. But where's Madam Rampant, and the rest of the ladies, Mr Rake-hell?

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Faith, sir, being disappointed at noon they were unwilling anymore to set a certainty at hazard. ’Tis Term-time and they have severally betook themselves, some to their chamber-practice and others to the places of public pleading.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Faith, brother Jolly, let us even go into an arbor and then feague Mr Rake-hell.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: With all my heart, would we had Madam Rampant.

lg.l: She's as frolic and free
As her lovers dare be,
Never awed by a foolish punctilio;
She'll not start from her place,
Though thou namest a black ace,
And will drink a beer glass to Spudilio.

sp.p: Hey, boys! Come, come, come! Let's in, and delay our sport no longer.

div2.stage: Exit singing “She'll not start from her place, etc.”

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Freeman!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Courtall, what the devil's the matter with thee? I have observed thee prying up and down the walks like a citizen's wife that has dropped her holiday pocket handkerchief.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What unlucky devil has brought thee hither?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I believe a better natured devil than yours, Courtall, if a leveret be better meat than an old puss that has been coursed by most of the young fellows of her country. I am not working my brain for a counter-plot, a disappointment is not my business.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You are mistaken, Freeman. Prithee be gone and leave me the garden to myself, or I shall grow as testy as an old fowler that is put by his shoot after he has crept half a mile upon his belly.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Prithee be thou gone, or I shall take it as unkindly as a chemist would if thou shouldst kick down his limbeck in the very minute that he looked for projection.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, you must yield, Freeman, your business cannot be of such consequence as mine.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: If ever thou hadst a business of such consequence in thy life as mine is I will condescend to be made incapable of affairs presently.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why, I have an appointment made me, man, without my seeking, by a woman for whom I would have mortgaged my whole estate to have had her abroad but to break a cheesecake.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: And I have an appointment made me without my seeking too, by such a she that I will break the whole Ten Commandments rather than disappoint her of her breaking one.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, you do but jest, Freeman, a forsaken mistress could not be more malicious than thou art. Prithee be gone.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Prithee do thou be gone.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Sdeath! The sight of thee will scare my woman forever.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: 'Sdeath! The sight of thee will make my woman believe me the falsest villain breathing.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: We shall stand fooling till we are both undone, and I know not how to help it.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Let us proceed honestly like friends, discover the truth of things to one another, and if we cannot reconcile our business we will draw cuts and part fairly.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I do not like that way, for talk is only allowable at the latter end of an intrigue and should never be used at the beginning of an amour for fear of frighting a young lady from her good intentions. Yet I care not, though I read the letter, but I will conceal the name.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I have a letter too and am content to do the same.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (Reads.) Sir, in sending you this letter I proceed against the modesty of our sex—

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: 'Sdeath, this begins just like my letter!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Do you read on then?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: (Reads.) But let not the good opinion I have conceived of you, make you too severe in your censuring of me—

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Word for word!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Now do you read again.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (Reads.) If you give yourself the trouble to be walking in the new Spring Garden this evening I will meet you there and tell you a secret which I have reason to fear, because it comes to your knowledge by my means, will make you hate your humble servant.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Verbatim my letter, heyday!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Prithee let’s compare the hands.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: 'Sdeath, the hand's the same!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I hope the name is not the same too...

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: If it be we are finely jilted, faith.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I long to be undeceived. Prithee do thou show first, Freeman.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: No, but both together, if you will.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Agreed.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Ariana.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Gatty. Ha, ha, ha!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: The little rogues are masculine in their proceedings and have made one another confidents in their love.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: But I do not like this altogether so well, Frank. I wish they had appointed us several places; for though 'tis evident they have trusted one another with the bargain, no woman ever seals before witness.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Prithee, how didst thou escape the snares of the old devil this afternoon?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: With much ado. Sentry had set me, if her ladyship had got me into her clutches there had been no getting off without a rescue or paying down the money, for she always arrests upon execution.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You made a handsome lie to her woman.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: For all this I know she's angry, for she thinks nothing a just excuse in these cases, though it were to save the forfeit of a man’s estate or reprieve the life of her own natural brother.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Faith, thou hast not done altogether like a gentleman with her. Thou shouldst fast thyself up to a stomach now and then to oblige her. If there were nothing in it but the hearty welcome, methinks 'twere enough to make thee bear sometimes with the homeliness of the fare.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I know not what I might do in a camp where there were no other woman. But I shall hardly in this town, where there is such plenty, forbear good meat to get myself an appetite to horse flesh.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: This is rather an aversion in thee than any real fault in the woman. If this lucky business had not fallen out, I intended with your good leave to have out-bid you for her ladyship’s favor.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I should never have consented to that, Frank. Though I am a little resty at present I am not such a jade, but I should strain if another rid against me. I have e'er now liked nothing in a woman that I have loved at last in spite only because another had a mind to her.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Yonder are a couple of vizards tripping towards us.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Tis they, i'faith!

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: We need not divide, since they come together.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I was a little afraid, when we compared letters, they had put a trick upon us; but now I am confirmed they are mighty honest.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: [To Gatty] We cannot avoid 'em.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: [To Ariana] Let us dissemble our knowledge of their business a little, and then take 'em down in the height of their assurance.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN AND COURTALL
sp.p: Your servant, ladies.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: I perceive it is as impossible, gentlemen, to walk without you as without our shadows: never were poor women so haunted by the ghosts of their self-murdered lovers.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: If it should be our good fortunes to have you in love with us, we will take care you shall not grow desperate and leave the world in an ill humor.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: If you should, certainly your ghosts would be very malicious.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Twere pity you should have your curtains drawn in the dead of the night and your pleasing slumbers interrupted by anything but flesh and blood, ladies.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Shall we walk a turn?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: By yourselves, if you please.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Our company may put a constraint upon you. For I find you daily hover about these gardens as a kite does about a backside, watching an opportunity to catch up the poultry.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Woe be to the daughter or wife of some merchant tailor, or poor felt-maker now; for you seldom row to Fox Hall without some such plot against the city.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You wrong us, ladies, our business has happily succeeded since we have the honor to wait upon you.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You could not expect to see us here.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Your true lover, madam, when he misses his mistress is as restless as a spaniel that has lost his master. He ranges up and down the plays, the park, and all the gardens, and never stays long but where he has the happiness to see her.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I suppose your mistress, Mr Courtall, is always the last woman you are acquainted with.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Do not think, madam, I have that false measure of my acquaintance which poets have of their verses, always to think the last best, though I esteem you so in justice to your merit.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Or if you do not love her best, you always love to talk of her most. As a barren coxcomb that wants discourse is ever entertaining company out of the last book he read in.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Now you accuse me most unjustly, madam. Who the devil, that has common sense will go a birding with a clack in his cap?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Nay, we do not blame you, gentlemen, everyone in their way: a huntsman talks of his dogs, a falconer of his hawks, a jockey of his horse, and a gallant of his mistress.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Without the allowance of this vanity, an amour would soon grow as dull as matrimony.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Whatsoever you say, ladies, I cannot believe you think us men of such abominable principles.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: For my part, I have ever held it as ingrateful to boast of the favors of a mistress as to deny the courtesies of a friend.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: A friend that bravely ventures his life in the field to serve me deserves but equally with a mistress that kindly exposes her honor to oblige me, especially when she does it as generously too, and with as little ceremony.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: And I would no more betray the honor of such a woman than I would the life of a man that should rob on purpose to supply me.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We believe you men of honor, and know it is below you to talk of any woman that deserves it.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: You are so generous you seldom insult after a victory.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: And so vain that you always triumph before it.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Sdeath! What's the meaning of all this?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Though you find us so kind, Mr Courtall, pray do not tell Mrs Gazette tomorrow that we came hither on purpose this evening to meet you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I would as soon print it and fee a fellow to post it up with the playbills.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You have reposed a great deal of confidence in her, for all you pretend this ill opinion of her secrecy now.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I never trusted her with the name of a mistress that I should be jealous of if I saw her receive fruit and go out of the playhouse with a stranger.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: For ought as I see we are infinitely obliged to you, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Tis impossible to be insensible of so much goodness, madam.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: What goodness, pray, sir?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Come, come, give over this raillery.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You are so ridiculously unworthy that 'twere a folly to reprove you with a serious look.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: On my conscience, your heart begins to fail you now we are coming to the point as a young fellow's that was never in the field before.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: You begin to amaze me.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Since you yourself sent the challenge, you must not in honor fly off now.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Challenge! Oh heavens! This confirms all: were I a man, I would kill thee for the injuries thou hast already done me.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: (to Ariana) Let not your suspicion of my unkindness make you thus scrupulous. Was ever city ill-treated that surrendered without assault or summons?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Dear sister, what ill spirit brought us hither? I never met with so much impudence in my life.

p.seg: Hey jilts! They are as good at it already as the old one, i'faith.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Come, ladies, you have exercised your wit enough. You would not venture letters of such consequence for a jest only.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Letters! Bless me, what will this come to?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: To that none of us shall have cause to repent I hope, madam.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Let us fly 'em, sister: they are devils and not men, they could never be so malicious else.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Your servant, cousins.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (Starting) Ho, my Lady Cockwood! My ears are grown an inch already!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: [To Gatty] My lady! she'll think this an appointment, sister.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: [To Courtall] This is Madam Machiavel, I suspect, Courtall.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Freeman] Nay, 'tis her plot doubtless. Now am I as much out of countenance as I should be if Sir Oliver should take me making bold with her ladyship.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Do not let me discompose you, I can walk alone, cousins.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Are you so uncharitable, madam, to think we have any business with 'em?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: It has been our ill fortune to meet 'em here, and nothing could be so lucky as your coming, madam, to free us from 'em.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: They have abused us in the grossest manner.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Counterfeited letters under our hands.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Never trouble yourselves, cousins, I have heard this is a common practice with such unworthy men. Did they not threaten to divulge them and defame you to the world?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We cannot believe they intend anything less, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Doubtless they had such a mean opinion of your wit and honor that they thought to fright you to a base compliance with their wicked purposes.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: I hate the very sight of 'em.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I could almost wish myself a disease to breathe infection upon 'em.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Very pretty! We have carried on our designs very luckily against these young ladies.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: We have lost their good opinion forever.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I know not whether their folly or their impudence be greater; they are not worth your anger, they are only fit to be laughed at and despised.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: A very fine old devil this!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Mr Freeman, this is not like a gentleman, to affront a couple of young ladies thus. But I cannot blame you so much, you are in a manner a stranger to our family. But I wonder how that base man can look me in the face, considering how civilly he has been treated at our house.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: The truth is, madam, I am a rascal, but I fear you have contributed to the making me so. Be not as unmerciful as the devil is to a poor sinner.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Did you ever see the like? Never trust me, if he has not the confidence to make my virtuous lady accessory to his wickedness.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Ay Sentry! ’Tis a miracle if my honor escapes, considering the access which his greatness with Sir Oliver has given him daily to me.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Faith, ladies, we did not counterfeit these letters, we are abused as well as you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I received mine from a porter at the King's Playhouse, and I will show it you that you may see if you know the hand.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [To Sentry] Sentry, are you sure they never saw any of your writing?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Sdeath! I am so discomposed I know not where I have put it.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: [To Lady Courtall] Oh madam! Now I remember myself, Mrs Gatty helped me once to indite a letter to my sweet-heart.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [To Sentry] Forgetful wench! Then I am undone!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Oh, here it is... Hey, who's here?

div2.stage: As he has the letter in hand, enter Sir Joslin, Sir Oliver and Rake-hell, all drunk, with Music.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN, SIR OLIVER, RAKE-HELL AND MUSIC

lg.l: (They sing.) She's no mistress of mine
That drinks not her wine,
Or frowns at my friends’ drinking motions;
If my heart thou would'st gain,
Drink thy bottle of champagne,
’Twill serve thee for paint and love potions.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Who's here? Courtall! In my lady's company! I'll dispatch him presently! Help me, brother Jolly!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: For heaven’s sake, Sir Oliver!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: (Drawing) What do you mean, sir?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I'll teach you more manners than to make your attempts on my lady, sir!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD AND SENTRY
sp.p: Oh! Murder! Murder!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Save my dear Sir Oliver! oh, my dear Sir Oliver!

div2.stage: The young ladies [Ariana, Gatty] shriek and run out; they all [Freeman, Sir Joslin, Rake-hell] draw to part 'em; they [Sir Oliver, Courtall] fight off the stage; she [Lady Cockwood] shrieks and runs out

div2.head: SCENE 1
div2.stage: Enter Lady Cockwood, table, and carpet.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
I did not think he had been so desperate in his drink. If they had kiled one another, I had then been revenged, and freed from all my fears... Enter Sentry.
Sentry, your carelessness and forgetfulness some time or other will undo me! Had not Sir Oliver and Sir Joslin came so luckily into the garden, the letters had been discovered and my honor left to the mercy of a false man and two young fleering girls. Did you speak to Mr Freeman unperceived in the hurry?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I did, madam, and he promised me to disengage himself as soon as possibly he could and wait upon your ladyship with all secrecy.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I have some reason to believe him a man of honor.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Methinks indeed his very look, madam, speaks him to be much more a gentleman than Mr Courtall. But I was unwilling before now to let your ladyship know my opinion for fear of offending your inclinations.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I hope by his means to get these letters into my own hands and so prevent the inconveniencies they may bring upon my honor.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I wonder, madam, what should be Sir Oliver's quarrel to Mr Courtall.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You know how apt he is to be suspicious in his drink. ’Tis very likely he thought Mr Courtall betrayed him at the Bear today.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Pray heaven he be not jealous of your ladyship, finding you abroad so unexpectedly. If he be, we shall have a sad hand of him when he comes home, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I should have apprehended it much myself, Sentry, if his drunkenness had not unadvisedly engaged him in his quarrel. As soon as he grows a little sober I am sure his fear will bring him home and make him apply himself to me with all humility and kindness. For he is ever under hand fain to use my interest and discretion to make friends to compound these businesses or to get an order for the securing his person and his honor.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I believe verily Mr Courtall would have been so rude to have killed him if Mr Freeman and the rest had not civilly interposed their weapons.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Heavens forbid! Though he be a wicked man, I am obliged in duty to love him. Whither did my cousins go after we came home, Sentry?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: They are at the next door, madam, laughing and playing at Lantrelou with my old Lady Love-youth and her daughters.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
I hope they will not come home then to interrupt my affairs with Mr Freeman. (Knocking without).
Hark, somebody knocks! It may be him, run down quickly.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I fly, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Now if he has a real inclination for my person I'll give him a handsome opportunity to reveal it.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Your servant, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh Mr Freeman! This unlucky accident has robbed me of all my quiet. I am almost distracted with thinking of the danger Sir Oliver's dear life is in.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You need not fear, madam, all things will be reconciled again tomorrow.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: You would not blame my lady's apprehensions, did you but know the tenderness of her affections.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Mr Courtall is a false and merciless man.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: He has always owned a great respect for your ladyship, and I never heard him mention you with the least dishonor.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: He cannot without injuring the truth, heaven knows my innocence. I hope you did not let him know, sir, of your coming hither.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I should never merit the happiness to wait upon you again had I so abused this extraordinary favor, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: If I have done anything unbeseeming my honor I hope you will be just, sir, and impute it to my fear. I know no man so proper to compose this unfortunate difference as yourself, and if a lady's tears and prayers have power to move you to compassion I know you will employ your utmost endeavor to preserve me and my dear Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Do not, madam, afflict yourself so much: I dare engage my life and his life and honor shall be both secure.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You are truly noble, sir. I was so distracted with my fears that I cannot well remember how we parted at the Spring Garden.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: We all divided, madam. After your ladyship and the young ladies were gone together, Sir Oliver, Sir Joslin, and the company with them took one boat, and Mr Courtall and I another.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Then I need not apprehend their meeting again tonight.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You need not, madam. I left Mr Courtall in his chamber, wondering what should make Sir Oliver draw upon him and fretting and fuming about the trick that was put upon us with the letters today.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p:
Oh! I had almost forgot myself. I assure you, sir, those letters were sent by one that has no inclination to be an enemy of yours. (Knocking below).
Somebody knocks. Exit Sentry.
If it be Sir Oliver I am undone, he will hate me mortally if he does but suspect I use any secret means to hinder him from justifying his reputation honorably to the world.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Oh madam! Here is Mr Courtall below in the entry, discharging a coachman. I told him your ladyship was busy but he would not hear me and I find, do what I can, he will come up.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I would not willingly suspect you, sir.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I have deceived him, madam, in my coming hither and am as unwilling he should find me here as you can be.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: He will not believe my innocent business with you but will raise a new scandal on my honor and publish it to the whole town.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Let him step into the closet, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Quick, sir, quick, I beseech you, I will send him away again immediately.

div2.stage: [Exit Freeman into the closet.] Enter Courtall.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Mr Courtall! Have you no sense of honor nor modesty left? After so many injuries to come into our house, and without my approbation rudely press upon my retirement thus?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Pray, madam, hear my business.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Thy business is maliciously to pursue my ruin. Thou com’st with a base design to have Sir Oliver catch thee here and destroy the only happiness I have.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I come, madam, to beg your pardon for the fault I did unwillingly commit, and to know of you the reason of Sir Oliver's quarrel to me.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Thy guilty conscience is able to tell thee that, vain and ungrateful man!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I am innocent, madam, of all things that may offend him. And I am sure, if you would but hear me, I should remove the justice of your quarrel too.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You are mistaken, sir, if you think I am concerned for your going to the Spring Garden this evening. My quarrel is the same with Sir Oliver, and is so just that thou deserv’st to be poisoned for what thou hast done.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Pray, madam, let me know my fault.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I blush to think upon’t. Sir Oliver, since we came from the Bear, has heard something thou hast said concerning me. But what it is I could not get him to discover. He told me 'twas enough for me to know he was satisfied of my innocence.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This is mere passion, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: This is the usual revenge of such base men as thou art, when they cannot compass their ends, with their venomous tongues to blast the honor of a lady.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: This is a sudden alteration, madam. Within these few hours you had a kinder opinion of me.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: 'Tis no wonder you brag of favors behind my back, that have the impudence to upbraid me with kindness to my face. Dost thou think I could ever have a good thought of thee, whom I have always found so treacherous in thy friendship to Sir Oliver?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Oh madam! Here is Sir Oliver come home!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: O heavens! I shall be believed guilty now and he will kill us both.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I warrant you, madam, I'll defend your life.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh! There will be murder, murder! For heaven’s sake, sir, hide yourself in some corner or other.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I'll step into that closet, madam.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Hold, hold, sir, by no means! His pipes and his tobacco box lie there, and he always goes in to fetch 'em.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Your malice will soon be at an end. Heaven knows what will be the fatal consequence of your being found here.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Madam, let him creep under the table, the carpet is long enough to hide him.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Have you good nature enough to save the life and reputation of a lady?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Anything to oblige you, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: (Running to the closet [to Freeman]) Be sure you do not stir, sir, whatsoever happens.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Not unless he pulls me out by the ears.

p.seg: Good! He thinks my lady speaks to him.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: My dear Sir Oliver—

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I am unworthy of this kindness, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Nay, I intend to chide you for your naughtiness anon, but I cannot choose but hug thee and kiss thee a little first. I was afraid I should never have had thee alive within these arms again.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Your goodness does so increase my shame I know not what to say, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Well, I am glad I have thee safe at home. I will lock thee up above in my chamber and will not so much as trust thee downstairs till there be an end of this quarrel.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I was so little myself I knew not what I did, else I had not exposed my person to so much danger before thy face.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: 'Twas cruelly done, sir, knowing the killing concerns my lady has for you.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: If Mr Courtall had killed thee I was resolved not to survive thee. But before I had died I would have dearly revenged thy murder.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p:
As soon as I had recollected myself a little I could not rest till I came home to give thee this satisfaction, that I will do nothing without thy advice and approbation, my dear. I know thy love makes thy life depend upon mine, and it is unreasonable I should upon my own rash head hazard that though it be for the justification of thy honor. [Knocks over a China orange on top of the table.]
Ud’s me! I have let fall a China orange that was recommended to me for one of the best that came over this year. 'Slife, light the candle, Sentry, 'tis run under the table.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh, I am not well!

div2.stage: Sentry takes up the candle, there is a great knocking at the door, she runs away with the candle.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Oh heaven! Who's that that knocks so hastily?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Why, Sentry! Bring back the candle! Are you mad to leave us in the dark, and your lady not well? How is it, my dear?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: For heaven’s sake, run after her, Sir Oliver! Snatch the candle out of her hand and teach her more manners.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: I will, my dear.

p.seg: What shall I do? Was ever woman so unfortunate in the management of affairs!
What will become of me now?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [Aside] It must be so, I had better trust my honor to the mercy of them two than be betrayed to my husband. Mr Courtall, give me your hand quickly, I beseech you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Here, here, madam. What's to be done now?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I will put you into the closet, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: He'll be coming in for his tobacco box and pipes.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Never fear that, sir.

p.seg: Now shall I be discovered! Pox on your honorable intrigue, would I were safe at Gifford’s.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Here, here, sir, this is the door: whatsoever you feel be not frighted, for should you make the least disturbance you will destroy the life and, what is more, the honor of an unfortunate lady.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: So, so, if you have occasion to remove again make no ceremony, madam.

div2.stage: [Exit Courtall into the closet.] Enter Sir Oliver, Sentry, Ariana, Gatty.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Here is the candle. How dost thou, my dear?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: I could not imagine, Sentry, you had been so ill-bred to run away and leave your master and me in the dark!

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I thought there had been another candle upon the table, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Good! You thought! You are always excusing of your carelessness. Such another misdemeanor—

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Prithee, my dear, forgive her.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: The truth is I ought not to be very angry with her at present, 'tis a good natured creature. She was so frighted for fear of thy being mischiefed in the Spring Garden that I verily believe she scarce knows what she does yet.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Light the candle, Sentry, that I may look for my orange.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: You have been at my Lady Love-youth’s, cousins, I hear.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: We have, madam.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: She charged us to remember her service to you.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: [Picks up the orange.] So, here it is, my dear, I brought it home on purpose for thee.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: 'Tis a lovely orange indeed! Thank you, my dear. I am so discomposed with the fright I have had that I would fain be at rest.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Get a candle, Sentry. Will you go to bed, my dear?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: With all my heart, Sir Oliver. ’Tis late, cousins, you had best retire to your chamber too.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We shall not stay long here, madam.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Come, my dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Good night, cousins.

sp.speaker: GATTY AND ARIANA
sp.p: Your servant, madam.

div2.stage: Exeunt Sir Oliver, Lady Cockwood, and Sentry.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: I cannot but think of those letters, sister.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: That is, you cannot but think of Mr Freeman, sister. I perceive he runs in thy head as much as a new gown uses to do in the country the night before 'tis expected from London.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: You need not talk, for I am sure the losses of an unlucky gamester are not more his meditation than Mr Courtall is yours.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: He has made some slight impression on my memory, I confess. But I hope a night will wear him out again as it does the noise of a fiddle after dancing.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Love, like some stains, will wear out of itself, I know, but not in such a little time as you talk of, sister.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: It cannot last longer than the stain of a mulberry at most. The next season out that goes, and my heart cannot be long unfruitful, sure.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Well, I cannot believe they forged these letters. What should be their end?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: That you may easily guess at. But methinks they took a very improper way to compass it.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: It looks more like the malice or jealousy of a woman than the design of two witty men.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: If this should prove a fetch of her ladyship’s now that is a-playing the loving hypocrite above with her dear Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: How unluckily we were interrupted when they were going to show us the hand!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: That might have discovered all. I have a small suspicion that there has been a little familiarity between her ladyship and Mr Courtall.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Our finding of 'em together in the Exchange, and several passages I observed at the Bear, have almost made me of the same opinion.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Yet I would fain believe the continuance of it is more her desire than his inclination. That which makes me mistrust him most is her knowing we made 'em an appointment.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: If she were jealous of Mr Courtall she would not be jealous of Mr Freeman too. They both pretend to have received letters.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: There is something in it more than we are able to imagine. Time will make it out, I hope, to the advantage of the gentlemen.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: I would gladly have it so. For I believe, should they give us a just cause, we should find it a hard task to hate them.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: How I love the song I learnt th'other day, since I saw them in the Mulberry Garden!

lg.l: To little or no purpose I spent many days,
In ranging the park, th'Exchange and th' plays;
For ne'er in my rambles till now did I prove
So lucky to meet with the man I could love.
Oh! how I am pleased when I think on this man,
That I find I must love, let me do what I can!
How long I shall love him, I can no more tell,
Than had I a fever when I should be well.
My passion shall kill me before I will show it,
And yet I would give all the world he did know it;
But oh, how I sigh when I think should he woo me,
I cannot deny what I know would undo me!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Fye, sister, thou art so wanton.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I hate to dissemble when I need not. ‘Twould look as affected in us to be reserved now w'are alone as for a player to maintain the character she acts in the tiring room.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Prithee sing a good song.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Now art thou for a melancholy madrigal, composed by some amorous coxcomb who swears in all companies he loves his mistress so well that he would not do her the injury were she willing to grant him the favor, and it may be is sot enough to believe he would oblige her in keeping his oath too.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Well, I will reach thee thy guitar out of the closet to take thee off of this subject.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I'd rather be a nun than a lover at thy rate. Devotion is not able to make me half so serious as love has made thee already.

div2.stage: Ariana opens the closet, Courtall and Freeman come out.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Ha, Freeman! Is this your business with a lawyer? Here's a new discovery, i'faith!

div2.stage: They [Ariana and Gatty] shriek and run out.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Peace, man! I will satisfy your jealousy hereafter. Since we have made this lucky discovery, let us mind the present businesses.

div2.stage: Courtall and Freeman catch the ladies and bring them back.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Nay, ladies, now we have caught you there is no escaping till w'are come to a right understanding.

div2.stage: Enter Lady Cockwood and Sir Oliver and Sentry.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Come, never blush, we are as loving as you can be for your hearts, I assure you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Had it not been our good fortunes to have been concealed here, you would have had ill nature enough to dissemble with us at least a fortnight longer.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: What's the matter with you here? Are you mad, cousins? Bless me, Mr Courtall and Mr Freeman in our house at these unseasonable hours?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Fetch me down my longsword, Sentry! I lay my life Courtall has been tempting the honor of the young ladies!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh, my dear!

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: We are almost scared out of our wits! My sister went to reach my guitar out of the closet and found 'em both shut up there.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Come, come, this will not serve your turn. I am afraid you had a design secretly to convey 'em into your chamber! Well, I will have no more of these doings in my family, my dear. Sir Joslin shall remove these girls tomorrow.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You injure the young ladies, madam. Their surprise shows their innocence.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: If anybody be to blame it is Mr. Sentry.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: What mean you, sir? Heaven knows I know no more of their being here—

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Nay, nay, Mrs Sentry, you need not be ashamed to own the doing of a couple of young gentlemen such a good office.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Do not think to put your tricks upon me, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Understanding by Mrs Sentry, madam, that these young ladies would very likely sit and talk in the dining room an hour before they went to bed of the accidents of the day, and being impatient to know whether that unlucky business which happened in the Spring Garden about the letters had quite destroyed our hopes of gaining their esteem, for a small sum of money Mr Freeman and I obtained the favor of her to shut us up where we might overhear 'em.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Is this the truth, Sentry?

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: I humbly beg your pardon, madam.

p.seg: A lady's honour is not safe that keeps a servant so subject to corruption! I will turn her out of my service for this.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Good! I was suspicious their businesses had been with my lady at first.

p.seg: Now will I be in charity with him again, for putting this off so handsomely.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hark you, my dear: shall I forbid Mr Courtall my house?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Oh! By no means, my dear. I had forgot to tell thee since I acquainted thee with that business, I have been discoursing with my Lady Love-youth and she blamed me infinitely for letting thee know it and laughed exceedingly at me, believing Mr Courtall intended thee no injury and told me 'twas only a harmless gallantry which his French breeding has used him to.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Faith, I am apt enough to believe it. For, on my conscience, he is a very honest fellow. Ned Courtall! How the devil came it about that thee and I fell to sa, sa, in the Spring Garden?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You are best able to resolve yourself that, Sir Oliver.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, the devil take me if I had the least unkindness for thee. Prithee let us embrace and kiss, and be as good friends as ever we were, dear rogue!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: I am so reasonable, Sir Oliver, that I will ask no other satisfaction for the injury you have done me.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Here's the letter, madam.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Sister, look here, do you know this hand?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: 'Tis Sentry’s!

p.seg: Oh heavens! I shall be ruined yet.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: She has been the contriver of all this mischief!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Nay, now you lay too much to her charge in this. She was but my lady's secretary, I assure you, she has discovered the whole plot to us.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: What does he mean?

p.seg: Will he betray me at last?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: My lady being in her nature severely virtuous is, it seems, offended at the innocent freedom you take in rambling up and down by yourselves. Which made her, out of a tenderness to your reputations, counterfeit these letters in hopes to fright you to that reservedness which she approves of.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: (Aside) This has almost redeemed my opinion of his honor. Cousins, the little regard you had to the good counsel I gave you puts me upon this business.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Pray, madam, what was it Mrs Gazette told you concerning us?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Nothing, nothing, cousins. What I told you of Mr Courtall, was mere invention, the better to carry on my design for your good.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Freeman! Pray, what brought you hither?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: A kind summons from her ladyship.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Why did you conceal it from me?

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I was afraid thy peevish jealousy might have destroyed the design I had of getting an opportunity to clear ourselves to the young ladies.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
Fortune has been our friend in that beyond expectation.
(To the ladies) I hope, ladies, you are satisfied of our innocence now.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Well, had you been found guilty of the letters we were resolved to have counterfeited two contracts under your hands and have suborned witnesses to swear 'em.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: That had been a full revenge. For I know you would think it as great a scandal to be thought to have an inclination for marriage as we should to be believed willing to take our freedom without it.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: The more probable thing, ladies, had been only to pretend a promise. We have now and then courage enough to venture so far for a valuable consideration.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: The truth is, such experienced gentlemen as you are seldom mortgage your persons without it be to redeem your estates.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: 'Tis a mercy we have 'scaped the mischief so long and are like to do penance only for our own sins. Most families are a wedding behind hand in the world, which makes so many young men fooled into wives to pay their father’s debts. All the happiness a gentleman can desire is to live at liberty till he be forced that way to pay his own.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: Ladies, you know we are not ignorant of the good intentions you have towards us. Pray, let us treat a little.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: I hope you are not in so desperate a condition as to have a good opinion of marriage, are you?

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: 'Tis to as little purpose to treat with us of anything under that, as it is for those kind ladies that have obliged you with a valuable consideration to challenge the performance of your promise.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Well, and how, my dear Ned, goes the business between you and these ladies? Are you like to drive a bargain?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: Faith, Sir Oliver, we are about it.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: And cannot agree, I warrant you. They are for having you take a lease for life, and you are for being tenants at will, Ned, is it not so?

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: These gentlemen have found it so convenient lying in lodgings they’ll hardly venture on the trouble of taking a house of their own.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: A pretty country seat, madam, with a handsome parcel of land and other necessaries belonging to't, may tempt us. But for a town tenement that has but one poor conveniency we are resolved we'll never deal.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Hark! My brother Jolly's come home!

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Now, gentlemen, you had best look to yourselves and come to an agreement with us quickly. For I'll lay my life, my uncle has brought home a couple of fresh chapmen that will out-bid you.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hey, boys!

lg.l: A catch and a glass,
A fiddle and a lass,
What more would an honest man have?
Hang your temperate sot,
Who would seem what he's not;
’Tis I am wise, he's but grave.

sp.p: What's here? Mr Courtall and Mr Freeman!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Oh man! Here has been the prettiest, the luckiest discovery on all sides! We are all good friends again.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Hark you, brother Cockwood, I have got Madam Rampant! Rake-hell and she are without.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Oh, heavens! Dear brother Jolly, send her away immediately, my lady has such an aversion to a naughty woman that she will swound if she does but see her.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p:
Faith, I was hard put to't, I wanted a lover; and rather than I would break my old wont I dressed up Rampant in a suit I bought off Rake-hell. Enter Rake-hell [and Rampant].
But since this good company's here, I'll send her away. My little Rake-hell, come hither. You see, here are two powerful rivals, therefore for fear of kicking or a worse disaster, take Rampant with you and be going quickly.

sp.speaker: RAKE-HELL
sp.p: Your humble servant, sir.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: You may hereafter spare yourself this labor, Sir Joslin. Mr Freeman and I have vowed ourselves humble servants to these ladies.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: I hope we shall have your approbation, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Nay, if you have a mind to commit matrimony, I'll send for a canonical sir shall dispatch you presently.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: You cannot do better.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: What think you of taking us in the humor? Consideration may be your foe, ladies.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: Come, gentlemen, I'll make you a fair proposition. Since you have made a discovery of our inclinations, my sister and I will be content to admit you in the quality of servants.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: And if after a month’s experience of your good behavior upon serious thoughts you have courage enough to engage further, we will accept of the challenge and believe you men of honor.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Well spoke, i'faith, girls! And is it a match, boys?

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: If the heart of man be not very deceitful, 'tis very likely it may be so.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: A month is a tedious time, and will be a dangerous trial of our resolutions. But I hope we shall not repent before marriage, whate'er we do after.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: How stand matters between you and your lady, brother Cockwood? Is there peace on all sides?

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Perfect concord, man. I will tell thee all that has happened since I parted from thee when we are alone 'twill make thee laugh heartily. Never man was so happy in a virtuous and a loving lady!

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Though I have led Sir Oliver astray this day or two, I hope you will not exclude me the act of oblivion, madam.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: The nigh relation I have to you, and the respect I know Sir Oliver has for you, makes me forget all that has passed, sir. But pray be not the occasion of any new transgressions.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: [To Courtall] I hope, Mr Courtall, since my endeavors to serve you have ruined me in the opinion of my lady, you will intercede for a reconciliation.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p:
[To Mrs Sentry] Most willingly, Mr. Sentry.
[To Lady Cockwood] Faith, madam, since things have fallen out so luckily, you must needs receive your woman into favor again.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: Her crime is unpardonable, sir.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Upon solemn protestations, madam, that the gentlemen’s intentions were honorable and having reason to believe the young ladies had no aversion to their inclinations, I was of opinion I should have been ill-natured if I had not assisted 'em in the removing those difficulties that delayed their happiness.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Come, come, girl, confess how many guineas prevailed upon your easy nature.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: Ten, an't please you, sir.

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: 'Slife, a sum able to corrupt an honest man in office! Faith you must forgive her, my dear.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: If it be your pleasure, Sir Oliver, I cannot but be obedient.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: [To Lady Cockwood] If Sir Oliver, madam, should ask me to see this gold, all may be discovered yet.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [To Mrs Sentry] If he does, I will give thee ten guineas out of my cabinet.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: [To Lady Cockwood] I shall take care to put him upon’t. ’Tis fit, that I who have bore all the blame, should have some reasonable reward for't.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Lady Cockwood] I hope, madam, you will not envy me the happiness I am to enjoy with your fair relation.

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [To Courtall] Your ingenuity and goodness, sir, have made a perfect atonement for you.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Lady Cockwood] Pray, madam, what was your business with Mr Freeman?

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [To Courtall] Only to oblige him to endeavor a reconciliation between you and Sir Oliver. For though I was resolved never to see your face again, it was death to me to think your life was in danger.

sp.speaker: MRS SENTRY
sp.p: What a miraculous come off is this, madam!

sp.speaker: LADY COCKWOOD
sp.p: [To Courtall] It has made me so truly sensible of those dangers to which an aspiring lady must daily expose her hono, that I am resolved to give over the great business of this town and hereafter modestly confine myself to the humble affairs of my own family.

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: [To Lady Cockwood] 'Tis a very pious resolution, madam, and the better to confirm you in it, pray entertain an able chaplain.

p.seg: Certainly Fortune was never before so unkind to the ambition of a lady!

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Come, boys, faith we will have a dance before we go to bed. Sly-girl and Mad-cap, give me your hands, that I may give 'em to these gentlemen; a parson shall join you e'er long, and then you will have authority to dance to some purpose. Brother Cockwood, take out your lady, I am for Mr. Sentry. We'll foot it and side it, my pretty little miss, and when we are aweary, we'll lie down and kiss. Play away, boys!

sp.speaker: COURTALL
sp.p: To Gatty Now shall I sleep as little without you as I should do with you. Madam, expectation makes me almost as restless as jealousy.

sp.speaker: FREEMAN
sp.p: [To Ariana] Faith, let us dispatch this business. Yet I never could find the pleasure of waiting for a dish of meat when a man was heartily hungry.

sp.speaker: GATTY
sp.p: Marrying in this heat would look as ill as fighting in your drink.

sp.speaker: ARIANA
sp.p: And be no more a proof of love, then th'other is of valor.

sp.speaker: SIR JOSLIN
sp.p: Never trouble your heads further. Since I perceive you are all agreed on the matter, let me alone to hasten the ceremony. Come, gentlemen, lead 'em to their chambers. Brother Cockwood, do you show the way with your lady. Ha, Mrs Sentry!

lg.l: I gave my love a green gown
I’th merry month of may
And down she fell as wantonly,
As a tumbler does at play.

sp.p: Hey boys! Lead away, boys!

sp.speaker: SIR OLIVER
sp.p: Give me thy hand, my virtuous, my dear. Henceforwards may our mutual loves increase, and when we are a bed, we'll sign the peace.
